subtopic: SHELL. CONTRACTS-THE SHEET METAL PRODUCTS COMPANY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of discussing for a moment or two a personal matter. In his remarks to this House a few days ago, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) referred to me as being connected with a concern known as the Sheet Metal Products Company of Canada, Limited. I am connected with that concern. I desire first to read to the House a letter I received from that company:	t
Toronto, March 10, 1916.
Hon. A. E. Kemp, M.P., P.C.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Kemp :
We are in receipt of a, marked copy of Hansard of the 7th instant, in which we find certain references made by Mr. Carvell to this company.
The facts in relation to our transactions with the Shell Committee, briefly, are as follows:
All of the business offered has been through regular channels. No one, except a regular official of this company, has either directly or indirectly, had any negotiations whatever in connection therewith.
Shortly after the war broke out we were asked to make certain articles which were particularly in our line of business, and which we understood were component parts intended for use in making shells for the British Government. We congratulated ourselves on being able to be of some service in this connection, and as opportunity offered we rendered what assistance we could by giving information to other manufacturers, whose experience in a similar class of work was not as broad as ours, resulting, we believe, in increased production on their part, which was most desirable.

We eo-operated with the Inspection Branch of the Shell Committee in affording facilities for training inspectors, whereby they familiarized themselves with their work, thus enabling them to inspect similar work which was being done in many other places, and this service was publicly acknowledged. It was also stated that this plant had been of immeinse value in overcoming difficulties in connection with the manufacture of articles referred to.
The total amount of business received from the Shell Committee, to which reference is made by Mr. Carvel!, is considered small from two standpoints. First, in respect to the total amount of the class of articles required by the Shell Committee, which were distributed through many factories in different parts of the country, and second, it is also unimportant from the standpoint of the volume of our regular business, being approximately but three per cent in the years for which delivery was expected.
We do not know that any useful purpose can be served by making reference to that part of the speech which assumed to deal with the technical side of the question, as those who have not an intimate knowledge In respect to manufacturing processes would scarcely appreciate this phase of the subject. Suffice it to say that what are commonly called " tin cups " are made from twenty-two gauge steel tinned. The articles called " clips " arts made from either brass or steel, in respect to both of which the combined operations, before completion are not less than thirty, all of which require to be of the most precise and exact character, and which fact, as those who know will understand, is common to the manufacture of all classes of ammunition.
The foregoing has reference to two articles. The third article, to which reference has been made, is what are known as " sockets ". We accepted this business for the reason that the information which came to us was that the production of shells was being considerably retarded for lack of this particular part.
The execution of the Shell Committee orders necessitated special concentration and attention of our chief mechanical experts and factory executives, and, to a large extent, impeded operations in connection with our regular business, which under other than war conditions we should have viewed from a different standpoint, being always convinced that breaking into the manufacture of new and intricate articles tends to a condition of affairs which gives unfavourable results.
We remain.
Yours very truly,
The Sheet Metal Products Co.
of Canada, Limited.
*	F. S. Corrigan,
General Manager.
So much for that. So far as the personal remarks of my hon. friend are concerned, I wish to quote from Hansard. On March 7, Hansard, page 1606, my hon. friend from Carleton, referring to me, made this statement :
I And that the Shell Committee purchased from a member of this Government $300,000 worth of goods.
And on Hansard, page 1607, he made the following statement:
I think the Shell Committee wlm were appointed by this Government, for this Government, and acting under the instructions of this Government, surely ought to exhaust every means of purchasing supplies before resorting to the members of the Government themselves.
Then, on page 1634, my hon. friend, still debating the same subject, on his responsibility as a member of this House made the statement that I was the manager of, or managed, this company. In the first place,
I desire to say that i have never at any time in my life received any favours from this Government or from any other Government of Canada. Secondly, for many years before becoming a member of this Government, I had taken no active part whatever in the management of this company. If all the time that I have given to the consideration of the affairs of this company since the war broke out was added together,
I am quite sure it would not amount to as much as half a day. I have not even been in the works of this company since the war broke out. The first specific information I had in regard to these shell contracts, so-called, was when I read the remarks of my hon. friend from Carleton in Hansard. I do not want anything that I am saying, or shall say, to be considered in any sense as an apology because this company accepted this business. If they had refused to accept this business because I was a member of this Government, such action on their part would have received my condemnation. I want to say further, that if I had been the means of having this company refuse to assist in making, munitions for the British Government, I would consider myself an object of contempt in this country,, and I would not, I believe, be considered a decent Canadian or a decent British subject.

Bill No. 26, respecting the Corporation of the City of Brantford-Mr. Cockshutt- in Committee.
Was this Bill explained?

The sections were all carried, except section 3. On consideration, this Bill has been found to be correct. The law clerk of the committee went into the matter thoroughly, and finds the Bill to be in correct form. In my opinion it should pass.

This seems .a rather
peculiar Bill. It seems to take the authority in a municipal matter into the hands of this Parliament. What is the real reason for having the Act passed in this form?

As I understand it, the Grand Valley Railway Company was chartered by Act of this Parliament. The city of Brantford is taking over and operating this railway, which is the road Tunning around the city of Brantford. The city is appointing a commission to operate the road. The authority of this Parliament is necessary for the transfer of the road from the Grand Valley Railway Company to this commission. The commission, of course, must operate the road upon the same conditions as those which governed the company. For instance, the company was obliged, under the Act, to pay municipal taxes to the several municipalities through which the Toad passes. When the Bill was before- the committee these municipalities were protected by inserting a clause to oblige the commission to carry out these conditions. The bon. member will see that the only way in which the commission can get its title is by an Act of this Parliament.

I understand that the company having been chartered by this Parliament, it would be necessary for this Parliament to give it power to perform acts not authorized by its charter. But whether this Parliament can give, or should assume to give, the city of Brantford power to do certain things is another matter. The corporation of the city of Brantford obtains its powers from the Ontario Legislature, and if those powers are to be altered one would think that the Ontario Legislature would be the proper authority to make the alteration.

As I understand it, legislation has been passed by the Ontario Legislature under which the municipality may take over this railway. But, if no provision were made by this Parliament, it would be free from the obligation to pay taxes to the other municipalities through which the road passes. It seems clear that this Parliament is the only authority that can empower the Grand Valley Railway Company to transfer its road to the commission appointed by the city of Brantford.

I understood from the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) that they had applied to the Provincial Legislature for the powers required from that authority. I do not think we have anything to do here with the by-laws of the city of Brantford.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think the Bill was submitted to the Department of Justice, and the department gave the opinion that it was within the jurisdiction 104	'
of this Parliament. It may be necessary to apply to the Legislature of Ontario also. As it is a railway subject to the jurisdiction of this Parliament, it would seem that the authority to own and operate it must come from this Parliament. In the case of a municipal corporation, it might be necessary also to obtain authority from the Provincial Legislature before legislation of this kind would be absolutely effective.

I think an Act has been passed by the Ontario Legislature, giving the city of Brantford the necessary powers in this case. My contention was that as the city of Brantford gets its powers from the Ontario Legislature, we scarcely have the right to give it any authority. If this Bill means that the federal authority will accept the city of Brantford as owner and operator of a federal road, in place of the company incorporated by this Parliament, that would be reasonable enough. But if it proposes to confer powers upon the city of Brantford, that seems to be a matter for the Legislature of Ontario. In section 1 I find these words:
The Corporation of the city , of Brantford, hereinafter called "the Corporation", may own, equip, operate, alter, maintain and manage the railway of the Grand Valley Railway Company.
I think this wording is a little awkward. If it means that Parliapient merely substitutes the words " city of Brantford " for " the Grand Valley Railway Company," I suppose the Bill is all right; but we have no right to give the city of Brantford any authority or to take any authority away from them.

in Committee.
On section 2-declaratory:

Where is this telephone
line?
The whole of the line of this company is in British Columbia.
An amendment has been introduced providing that the company may not operate in any other provinces without the consent of those provinces.

When these amendments are reprinted, I suggest that they be distributed so that we may consider them in an intelligent way. This Bill was reprinted.
. REVISED EDITION

as were several others, but the original Bills are still on our files.
Some of the western provinces have their own telephone companies. Was any question raised by the province of British Columbia as to its right to grant this charter?

That matter was taken
up, and an amending section put in.
I am afraid we do not know much about it.
I think we are all at sea, and wasting much time by not having these Bills printed.
If a Bill of this kind were introduced with reference to Ontario, a protest would come from Ontario members that these franchises ought to be granted by the provincial authorities.

This is the new section:
15a. Notwithstanding anything contained in this act, the Company shall not construct, operate, or maintain lines of telephones other than long distance lines in the city of Prince Rupert without having first obtained the consent of the municipality of the said city, or in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba without first having obtained the consent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council of the provinces in which it is proposed to construct, operate and maintain a line of telephone as aforesaid; but this restriction shall not apply to the construction, operation or maintainance of long distance lines of the Company into or through the said city of Prince Rupert, or into or through any or all of the said provinces.

That hardly meets the point I had in mind. What I ask is: has it been suggested on behalf of the province that this charter. should be granted not by the Federal authorities, hut by the pro

incial authorities? If it were definitely stated that it was the intention to run lines through other provinces, I should recognize the necessity of a federal charter; but in view of the fact that the operations of the company are evidently to be confined to the Province of British Columbia, I am surprised that some member from that province has not suggested that the charter should be dealt with by the provincial authorities.

This is not a new company; it is an old, established company that has been doing business in British Columbia for some years. I think the company controls practically the whole telephone service in that province. It is getting a Fed-

eral charter because the company wishes to connect with the United States, and with the long distance services in Alberta and Saskatchewan.

I notice that the amendment provides for an extension of long distance lines through any of the prairie provinces. There may he no objection to that, but, having regard to the fact that the telephone lines in the three prairie provinces. are practically under local government control, I think that the Bill should he reprinted with the amendment as agreed to in the Railway Committee, so that the Governments of these provinces may have an opportunity of seeing what the Bill says, and, what it does not say.
There is no objection to that.

The Bill was reprinted and distributed among members of the House; subsequently these amendments were presented to and finally passed by the committee. It was suggested that the Bill be further re-printed, but the committee decided otherwise because it had been once re-printed for the consideration of the members. There is no objection to its being reprinted.

I would urge very strongly that the Bill be re-printed and that it be held in committee until the Governments of those three provinces have at least had an opportunity of expressing an opinion as to whether it would in any 'way interfere with the management of their provincial telephone systems.

As the Bill now stands it does not in any way interfere with the provincial systems. It is not likely that any of the three prairie provinces would object to the construction of these lines right through their province without the company doing any businss in the province, in order to connect, say, with an Ontario line, or one in the United States. Perhaps the hon. member would wire to the Government of his province and ascertain whether there would he 'any objection. Every precaution is taken to protect the Provincial Governments' telephone systems.

ELECTIONS.	.	.
Is there a rule in the Post Office Department forbidding- postmasters from taking pa t in municipal elections as candidates, and from sitting as councillors and mayors?

An Order in Council was passed in 1893, prohibiting postmasters of incorporated towns from accepting appointment to representative positions as mayor, aldermen, or trustee of public or separate schools. It may be stated, however, that this Order in Council has only been strictly enforced as regards the larger cities. As regards the smaller incorporated towns and villages the department has not pressed the point, except where it was considered that the municipal duties might conflict or interfere with the duties of the postmaster.

1.	Is the post office at New Richmond West, Quebec, said to have been lately closed, to remain so closed, or is it to he re-opened?
2.	Are rural mail boxes looked or do they remain open?

1. The post office of New Richmond West, Quebec, was lately closed, following the

inauguration of rural mail delivery in that locality. Bequests have been received that the closing of the post office be reconsidered, and the same are now under investigation.
2. Not locked, as it might impede the efficiency of the service, especially in winter. Mr. E. M. MACDONALD (Pictou) moved for:
A copy of the pension list in force in Canada for disabled soldiers and of all petitions, letters or other documents relating to the amendment readjustment of the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am moving this motion for the purpose of urging upon the Government the desirability of making some changes in the pension list which was brought down at the last session of Parlia-

ment. Hon. gentlemen will recall tjiat the pension list at present in force for disabled soldiers was fixed by the terms of an Order in Council which was laid on the table of the House some two or three weeks before prorogation last year. These provisions went into effect without the subject having been referred to a committee of this House, or without it having come before the House for consideration in any formal way.
There are certain anomalies in connection with this pension list which have attracted attention throughout the country. I suppose that hon. gentlemen, ineluding members of the Government, have received a copy of a pamphlet which a committee of the Toronto Board of Trade has prepared dealing with this subject and which points out anomalies and makes recommendations which have been adopted and approved by the Toronto Board of Trade. I think hon. gentlemen will agree that one of our essential duties in connection with the war is the establishment of a fair pension list. A careful examination of the present .arrangement reveals a number of anomalies which require remedying. In the first place, I think that the four distinctions or degrees contained in the present pension list are anomalous. The first degree is applicable to those who are rendered totally incapable of earning a livelihood by reason of wounds contracted in action, or in the presence of the enemy. The second degree is applicable to those who are totally incapable of earning a livelihood on account of injuries received on active service, in thrill, or training, or who are rendered materially incapable as a result of wounds or injuries received, or illness contracted, in action, or in the presence of the enemy. I do not think there is any real reason why we should distinguish between these men who have ' been so unfortunate as to be rendered totally incapable. If a man volunteers in good faith to serve his country, and receives wounds which render him absolutely incapable, it does not matter to him in after life whether he received those wounds in the presence of the enemy or in training at home, and it ought not to make any difference in his pension. Only the other day there was a case in Toronto of an officer being rendered totally incapable for life as the result of an .accident while teaching his men how to throw bombs. That man is entitled to just as much consideration as if he had received his wounds in the presence of the enemy, and I submit that we
should make no distinction at all between men who are rendered totally incapable on active service and those who are rendered totally incapable by reason of injuries sustained on service in Canada.
It is also pointed out in this pamphlet that the present pension allowed to the men of the rank and file is too low, and a little later on I shall draw attention to the distinction that is made between the rank and file and the officers. The difference is in my opinion entirely too great. The pamphlet points out that while there is a difference in the pension allowed to privates and officers in Australia, the difference is not nearly so great as it is in Canada. We all know that in the Canadian expeditionary forces there are men in the rank and file of just as good social position, and just as intelligent, as are the officers. While I concede that we must make some distinction between a private and an officer, I submit that the difference in pension allowed under the present arrangement is entirely too great, and that the pensions to these two classes ought to be brought closer together, as in Australia.

This, of course, is a phase of the whole question of what we are to do with the soldiers who return.

Another suggestion has bqen brought to my .attention., the working out of which, perhaps, may be difficult so far as company railways are .concerned, but which might be applied to the Government railways. The suggestion is that men enlisted for overseas service be granted, when leave is given them to visit their homes, a rate of one cent a mile on the Government railways. Of course, it would be a . matter of certificates on the part of the officer granting the leave. It is suggested, also, that where .soldiers are travelling on the Government railway, going to or from their homes for recruiting purposes, or to visit their families before going overseas, they should be given concessions upon the dining-cars of the Government railways. It certainly seems anomalous that we should coax -and plead with the young fellow in the country town to go and fight for his country, and then when he consents, take him to a camp a 'hundred or two hundred miles away from his home; and, that when he wishes [DOT] to return to his home to visit his mother or his relatives under leave of his commanding officer, the Government railway should demand from him the last cent by way of fare. The Minister of Railways announced a very handsome surplus the other night. Here is a matter which would mean a great deal to the boys who have enlisted, and who wish to return to their homes. Some consideration should be shown them by the Government railways. This, of course, is aside from the main subject I desire to deal with in the resolution.
I bring these suggestions in Tegard to the pension law to the attention of the Govern*5 ment, feeling that the desire of us all would be to deal in an absolutely fair and equitable way with the unfortunate soldiers who return wounded. I trust the suggestions I have made will meet with favourable consideration by the Government, and that the anomalies which I think exist will be removed, and the whole pension system be placed upon a permanent basis by the establishment of a non-partisan pension board.

I will not go over the ground so well traversed by my hon. friend from iPictou (Mr. Macdonald). As to the general question of the scale of pensions, it will be generally agreed, I think, after reading the careful memorandum prepared by the Committee of Citizens in Toronto, that the scale pro-

vided last summer needs revision. No doubt it will receive it. A general revision upward, as well as a general equalization according to the suggestions made by the committee, will, I feel assured, receive adequate support in the House.
The matter of dealing with the pensions through a pensions board should, I think, receive the immediate attention of the Government. This question of pensions is one of such tremendous importance to the individual affected, and to the country at large, that it cannot be placed upon a permanent foundation, and cannot be put into fully [DOT] accredited and non-partisan hands too soon to meet the needs of the case or the views of the people. If I were to offer any criticism, it would be that we have hardly appreciated how deeply we are engaged in this war and how terrible are the effects of it that have already been felt. I read that our losses up to the present time have been
20,000	men in killed, wounded and missing. That means the provisions of the pension law -are in urgent demand at the moment, not only for the well-being of those who have suffered, but for the purpose of assuring those whom we are calling upon to offer themselves in our service, 'and their relatives and friends as well, that the country is absolutely behind them and will see that, whatever happens to them, they will be cared for, so far as the country can care for them, along certain well recognized and approved lines, and by means that will leave no room for question. It seems to me that we have been slow in appreciating how urgent this matter is, how far-reaching it is, and how tremendous the interests are that .depend upon it being adequately and .promptly handled.
I wish to allude in particular to two features of the care of returned soldiers. Some time ago I asked for certain Orders in Council which were brought down, and which I have before me. One is dated December 25, 1915, and makes provision for a gratuity of $100 in case of the discharge of a soldier only slightly disabled.
I can quite appreciate that there are conditions under which such a payment would be proper and adequate. But I wish to point out that, having regard to the memorandum attached to the Order in 'Council, this provision gives to a board which is not endowed with the fullest responsibility, and which, perhaps, has not the fullest knowledge of the facts, an opportunity to do less than justice to the discharged soldier. I do not like the wording of the

memorandum of information upon \yhich ithe Order in Council is ibased. The suggestion, as it appears to me, is that this provision offers a ready means of getting rid of a troublesome man and a troublesome question. I may be wrong in putting that interpretation upon this memorandum.

Wo feel, however, that it this man once gets his name on the pension list, it will be very difficult to cease paying him a p-rsion of a small amount, and therefore we feel that if we had the power to grant a man a gratuity in lieu of the pension, and if the T.easury Board would waive its rights in the case of the gratuity only, to say whether it would confirm our recommendation, we would be in a position to close the matter up without delay, whereas, under the present regulation, if we had the power to grant a gratuity, the whole matter has to be left open until a reply comes back from Oltawa.
The intention evidently is to close the man out with $100 for the convenience of the present Pensions Board. If I have misinterpreted the memorandum I will he glad, hut that is the impression it conveys to my mind, and I take the liberty of drawing the attention of the Government to it, and of voicing my views that that is not a proper attitude of mind in which to approach this question.
The next point that I wish to draw attention to is an Order in Council, dated December 16, 1915, making provision for men who have become insane in active service. I had occasion to mention this matter once before in the House, and I take the liberty of referring to it again, because it seems to me that the intent of this Order in Council
jars upon the sensibilities of the people at large. In this war, carried on with weapons such as are now used, it frequently occurs that men come out of the fight with their minds shattered, although physically they have not suffered injury. These men were physically perfect before they went in, and presumably they were mentally perfect as well. They have suffered such shock to their nervous system as has unbalanced their mind,s. It is a reasonable probability that such men, given favourable conditions, would make complete recovery of their reason and again become useful citizens, each one an asset to the state, and a benefit to himself and to his relatives. It was with a feeling which jarred upon my mind that I read in the newspapers that men in such cases were being committed to the ordinary asylums for treatment and consideration. I find that provision is made, under an Order in Council of December 16, for committment of such men to lunatic asylums. I wish to urge upon the Government as strongly as I can that this is not proper treatment to give to men in such circumstances. Their condition demands certain treatments and the best that the country can find for them, in the hope of recovering their intellects for the benefit of the country and the advantage of their relatives. I hope that special provision will be made, that institutions will he organized immediately, if they have not been organized already, for the special care of such cases as these. These men, in the perfection of physical health, have had their intellects unbalanced by reason of physical shock, and it is not unreasonable to hope that with proper care and treatment they may recover their intellects. I assure the Government that the public look, may I say, with horror, upon the fact that a young man who has volunteered as a soldier and who has suffered in this way is committed to an ordinary insane asylum where the surroundings naturally tend to militate against his ultimate recovery. In any case there is a certain, amount of sentiment in these things, as there ought to he, and we can surely better afford to spend a reasonable sum of money in making special provision for this new class of cases that has arisen in this war, than to be considered guilty of an insufficient regard for the sacrifices these men have made or the possibility of their recovering from the result of these sacrifices.

speechtext:
The subject of pensions has been under the consideration of the Government for

some time past, and probably it would have been taken up at an earlier date had it not been that I thought it desirable,-as this motion has been standing for some time upon the Order Paper,-that we should hear the views of hon. gentlemen before the Government took any definite or final action on the whole subject. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has brought the subject up in a very considerate and reasonable way. It is perfectly true that before the Order in Council which establishes the present scale of pensions was passed, we placed a draft of it upon the table of the House last session, and I requested an expression of the views of hon. members, in order that the Government might take it into consideration before the subject was dealt with by passing the Order in Council. Not a great of attention was given to it during the session, and perhaps it might have been better if the draft Order in 'Council had been printed and. circulated among the members, in order that the subject would thus more fully engage their attention. I shall have these papers brought down at once; I have been gathering them together. Then if opportunity for further debating .the matter is desired, the Government will be very glad to afford that opportunity, because the papers as brought down will embrace some suggestions and reports which have not yet been made -public. Among these there is a report, in the form of a letter to the Minister of Militia, from the chair*- man of the Pensions and Claims Board, Canadian Expeditionary Force, of which 6i.r Montague Allan is the chairman.
It is perfectly true that the scale which was submitted to the House last session, and which was authorized ' by Order in Council, does not proceed precisely upon the lines of the Australian pension list, but it follows that list very closely, except in one respect, to which I shall allude later. For totally disabled soldiers who have become incapacitated in active service, the scale for an unmarried soldier in Canada is $264; in Australia, $253; and in Great Britain, $316. The scale in Canada is slightly higher than that of Australia, and is about $50 lower than that of Great Britain. For a married soldier and wife, without children, the scale in Canada is $396; in Australia, $380; and in Great Britain, $316. The British scale makes no allowance for the fact that a man has a wife dependent upon him. For a soldier with a wife and one child, the scale in Canada is $456; in

Australia, $443; and in Great Britain, $348. There is an allowance made in Great Britain of $32 for the support of a child, but no allowance is made for the support of the wife. For a soldier totally incapacitated who has a wife and two children dependent upon him, the scale in Canada is $516; in Australia, $506; and in Great Britain, $380. That is to say, the scale in Canada is $10 more than in Australia, and $136 more than in Great Britain.
For a soldier, totally incapacitated, with a wife and three children dependent upon him, the scale in Canada is $576; in Australia $569, and in Great Britain $412. The Canadian scale, in this respect, is slightly higher than that in Australia, and $164 a year higher than that provided in Great Britain. For a soldier with a wife and four children dependent upon him, the scale in Canada is $637; in Australia $633, and in Great Britain $444; the Canadian scale being slightly higher than that of Australia, and nearly $200 greater than that of Great Britain. So it runs all through, except that, in Great Britain, and Australia, there is a difference in scale for the higher ranks.
My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has alluded to the fact that there is less difference in Australia than there is in Canada between the rates fixed for . privates and officers. That is true, but it does not arise by reason of the rates for the private soldier being lower in Canada, but by reason of the rates for oflicers in Canada being higher than in Australia. On the other hand, the pension rates for officers in Great Britain are on a considerably higher scale than they are in Canada, and on a very much higher scale than they are in Australia. For example, an unmarried lieutenant colonel in Canada, who has become totally incapacitated receives $1,200 as a pension; in Australia he receives $638, and in Great Britain $3,000. A major, totally incapacitated, receives in Canada, if he is an unmarried man, $960; in Australia $565, and in Great Britain $2,000. A captain who' is unmarried, and becomes totally incapacitated on active service, receives in Canada a pension of $720; in Australia $492, and in Great Britain $1,000. For a lieutenant, totally incapacitated, and unmarried, Canada provides $482; Australia $443, and Great Britain $700. A warrant officer, unmarried, and totally incapacitated receives in Canada $480; in Australia $377, and in Great Britain $506. For a sergeant totally incapacitated, and having no wife, Canada provides $336; Australia $340, and Great Britain $366.

My hon. friend from Pictou also adverted to the very considerable disparity between the provision made for single men and that for married men in this country, and he pointed out, I think with some force, that a married man who has a wife and three children, and who has become totally incapacitated, would, upon the death of his wife, receive a smaller pension than when his wife was living, although it might be very much more difficult in that case for him to take care of his
5 p.m. children and to support the family than it was before. I think that that ought to be taken into consideration. Of course, .unless the wife undertakes some work for the purpose of assisting in the support of her family, it is necessary to make provision for her maintenance. The wife, as well as the children, must be provided for in some way, and in fixing the pension scale, as we have established it in Canada, we proceeded very much along the lines which have been followed in Australia. We adhered much more closely to what has been done in Australia, than to what has been done in Great Britain, because it seemed to us that the conditions of this country were in that respect more similar to those of Australia than to those of Great Britain. Therefore, we thought we would be safer to follow the Australian than the British precedent.
It is said, I believe, in the report of the committee, of which Mr. Darling is chairman, that the Canadian rates for totally incapacitated single men are lower than elsewhere. That is not strictly accurate, when baldly stated in that way. I have already read the rates fixed in this country, in Australia, and in Great Britain. The rates in Canada for married men are larger than they are in Australia, and considerably larger than they are in Great Britain. It is true that for unmarried men, totally incapacitated, the rate in Canada is lower than in Great Britain, but it is not lower than the rate in Australia.
My hon. friend alluded to the necessity of a pensions board. It might be just as well that I should explain to the House how the Pensions Board was established, and who composes it. The present Pensions and Claims Board was authorized by a Militia Order, as were the several similar boards which preceded it, and it is now acting in virtue of Militia Order No. 366 of 2nd August, 1915, which reads:
The Pensions and Claims Board is reconstituted as follows: President-Col. J. S. Dunbar, Assistant Adjutant-General, Militia Headquarters ; members,-Lt. Col. C. W. Belton Permanent Army Medical Corps, and Honorary Lt. Col. C. L. Panet, secretary of the Department of Militia and Defence.
Lt.-Col. Belton is a medical officer who is attached to the board in that capacity, and he has been for a number of years in the permanent corps. After being passed upon by the board, the pension claims come in the form of a recommendation to the Governor in Council, and are taken into consideration by the Treasury Board in the first instance. The Governor in Council, under the provisions of the Order in Council which was passed last year, has the power to consider individual cases, but these individual cases are only considered upon a report first made by the Pensions Board. The section of the Order in Council to which I allude is:
597. Individual cases, for which the regulations do not provide or sufficiently provide, may be specially considered by the .Governor in' Council.
The procedure is, to have all such claims* submitted, in the first instance, to the Pensions Board, and to have the report of the Pensions Board thereon come before the Treasury Board. The Treasury Board may ask for such further information as it may desire, and may refer the case back for further consideration to the Pensions Board. In the end the recommendation of the Pensions Board, as adopted by the Treasury Board, comes to the Governor in Council and is passed in that way. The very fact that the Treasury Board had several cases of that kind early last autumn, seemed to impose upon it duties of so onerous a character, and to consume so large a portion of its time, that the question was mooted as to the establishment of a permanent 'Pensions Board, which would receive a report from the Departmental Pensions Board, and upon whose report the Governor in Council would be authorized to act. Some inquiry into the desirability of that method of procedure was made, and a document which will be brought down amongst the other papers was submitted to the Government; but as the session came on shortly afterwards, and as it was not only desirable but apparent that the subject would be debated in this House, no action has been taken up to the present time.	'
As to securing a method by which political influence of any kind, or pressure of an undesirable character might have no scope or effect, I am entirely at one with my hon. friend from Pictou, and I think that it is eminently important. I do not

think that anything of the kind has taken place under the board at present constituted. No minister of the Crown or member of Parliament, so far as I am aware, has interferred in these matters in any way whatever. If anything of the kind has taken place it has not come to my knowledge. I am informed that Lieut.-Colonel Dunbar, who has been for a very considerable time in the permanent service, is a gentleman with legal training in the first instance, and that he is capable of discharging, and does- discharge, the duties of Chairman of that Board very efficiently and very impartially. One of the other two members is a medical officer who has been for some time in the permanent service, and the other is Honorary Lieut.-Colonel Panet, who has also been a considerable time in the permanent service.
I endeavoured to get information as to the precise methods by which pensions are dealt with in the United Kingdom, but it was apparent to me that the various bodies which there deal with this subject had not been thoroughly co-ordinated up to that time, and that perhaps we could not derive benefit from any example which they could give us. A desirable thing, if we could accomplish it, would probably be to have a pensions board to deal not only with military pensions, but with naval pensions,' and to have it established under the conditions outlined by my hon. friend from Pictou.
With respect to soldiers' homes, I really have not had that matter brought very much to my personal attention. My knowledge of what is being done In this country, and indeed on the other side of the ocean, is almost wholly confined to the so-called convalescent homes. I do know, however, that the Military Hospitals and Convalescent Homes Commission have been making a pretty thorough study of conditions in Canada and in the United Kingdom, and I was informed a few days ago that Mr. W. M. Dobell, of Quebec, who [DOT]has been making a study of this suhject in the United Kingdom and also in France, had embodied certain views in a report that he had submitted to his colleagues of the Military Hospital and Convalescent Homes Commission, and that these views were now under consideration by that commission. On the whole, I gathered the impression that Mr. Dobell was of the opinion that too much had been done in the way of convalescent homes along cer-

tain lines; that perhaps some improvement might be made not only here but elsewhere, and that the view he expressed in the report was entirely in consonance with the view taken by the military authorities of Great Britain and of France. However, it is rather premature to speak of that.
My hon. friend from Pictou also spoke about the desirability of making special rates for soldiers who are enlisted in the overseas forces, and who might from time to time desire to visit their families. I should be very glad to commend that suggestion to the Minister of Railways and to see whether it cannot be carried out.
My hon. friend, from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) spoke of an Order in Council, which had not come to my attention until recently. I think it was passed when I was unwell. I am not aware of its exact phraseology, but it hardly seems to me that it would bear the construction which he puts upon it. I observe that the concluding paragraph of the report on which that Order in Council is based is expressed in these words:
We have a very good precedent before us, as the Imperial Service grants such gratuities.
It is, I think, the practice of the Pensions Board here to recommend a gratuity in addition to the pensions, in occasional cases of destitution or urgent need. In any case, if I understand the military regulations-I am always a little apprehensive about expressing an opinion with regard to them-the acceptance by any man of a gratuity would not debar him of the right to have a board called subsequently to consider his case, if it was apparent that his injury or disablement was greater than had been thought at first. I believe it is competent to any man to have a board called at any time for that purpose, and I think that a board can also be called at any time to have it established that a man to whom a pension has been granted has recovered his health, and that the pension to which he was entitled during the period of ihis disablement -should no longer be continued.
With regard to the whole question, I entirely agree with the view that we must give reasonable and even generous consideration to the claims of those who have gone to fight the battles of the Empire in this war, and who have shown their willingness to make the supreme sacrifice; reasonable and generous consideration to the dependents of those who have gone to the front and made that sacrifice, in

order	that this	Empire, the ideals
which it represents, and the institutions we enjoy,	may be preserved
for us and for future generations.
The report from the Pensions and 'Claims Board in Great Britain suggests a more elaborate scheme of analysis of the degrees of disablement. I think they divided them into six degrees by percentages: a man totally disabled would be classed 100 per cent; then they endeavoured to estimate those who have been disabled to the extent of 80 per cent, 60 per cent, 40 per cent, 20 per cent, and under 20 per cent. Then they lay down this principle:
All pensions to members of the .Canadian Militia disabled on active service should be awarded in direct proportion to the impairment of. capacity for earning a livelihood in the general market for untrained labour.
The note which they attach to that is this:
Men enlisting for active service in the Canadian militia as privates bring to the service of the country a healthy body. The previous - occupation of the recruit is not recognized as having any reference to the service which the soldier could give the State, unless it secures for him a higher rank than that of private, in which case the return made to him by the State in pay and pension is proportionately increased. The private soldier then is looked upon as offering merely a healthy mind and body to the public service. For practical purposes the market for healthy bodies is said to be the " general market for untrained labour."
It is to be noted that the amount of pension depends upon the impairment of capacity for earning a livelihood without reference to the former occupation and income of the soldier. That view will form part of the return to be brought down for the consideration of hon.gentlemenopposite.
There would be the case of men who, while incapacitated for performing the duties which they had hitherto performed in the community in which they live, might become capable, through vocational training, of performing other duties so that they could, at least in part, earn their livelihood. One of the duties which the Government ought to undertake in connection with any pension scheme is to make it possible, so far as we reasonably can, for men who have been disabled from taking part in any occupation in which they had been previously engaged, to take up some other occupation by which they may assist in earning their own livelihood. It is not in the interest of any citizen, who has served in the overseas forces and who is still capable of filling an active and useful part in the national life, to be placed in such a situation as to have no incentive whatever to do that work for which he may be fitted either through his own efforts alone or with assistance from the state. I have been impressed all along with the importance, in connection with this whole question, of doing the utmost that we can, by investigating methods on the other side ot the ocean and by thinking out methods for ourselves, to evolve a system by which all those who are not absolutely incapacitated but who are incapacitated to such an extent as to make it impossible for them to earn their livelihood in the way in which they formerly earned it, should be afforded the opportunity I have indicated. I believe that a certain committee of the Military Hospitals and Convalescent Homes Commission is studying that question very carefully, and that committee will probably be able, in the early future, to make some recommendations to the Government. I entirely agree that any appropriation that might be necessary for the carrying out of a scheme of that kind in a reasonable and effective way, would be money well spent by this country, first, in making the men to whom such an opportunity would be afforded, better citizens than they otherwise would be, and secondly, in the contribution which it would make to the general welfare and development of the country by increasing that much the earning capacity of the whole nation.
I shall be glad, as I have said before, after these papers are brought down, as they will be without a moment's delay, to move at once that they be printed for the information of hon. gentlemen, and after that is done, if my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) or any other gentleman should desire to have further debate, we would welcome it. Indeed, if a debate were not started otherwise, I think we should initiate it ourselves in order that the views of hon. gentlemen, which certainly must be of some assistance to the Government, might be elicited, and the Government be thus placed in a better position to deal with the whole subject.

(North Oxford) I am very glad to hear the Premier say that he believes ini vocational training, and I am sorry he was not here the other day when that question was under discussion. It was argued that these men 'be assisted by the Government educating them in such trades or callings as they might be fitted for, so that they would do something at least towards earning their own livelihood. I am also pleased that the

Premier will afford an opportunity for further discussion of this subject. I do not think I am giving away any secret of the Hospitals Commission when I say that Mr. Dobell told me that, in France, 80 per cent of these classed as totally 'disabled were', through vocational schools, being taught at least partly to earn their living. His statement only corroborates what I thought myself and what I had read in regard to those schools in France. I have been studying the question very carefully, and I am glad that the Premier endorses my views and that the Government will do everything possible to assist ill the establishment of schools of that character.
In reference to the pension scheme, I think the pension for the unmarried man who is totally disabled is slightly too low, and I would suggest raising it to a dollar a day, or $30 a month, and allotting the other pensions in proportion. I think the differences in the pension list are fairly well arranged. After the Premier has the information which he says he will bring down, it would be a good thing to appoint a small committee of members from both sides to study the question carefully and to report to the House, because the question is very important and means the expenditure of a great deal of money. I am sure the Government appreciates the fact that the question is of great importance and one that should not enter into politics at all.
I would also like to make a recommendation to the Government as to the personnel of the Pension Board. I do not say that the gentlemen now acting are not absolutely non-political; I do not know anything about them. But, no matter who the Pension Board, may be, in my judgment the matter must be taken out of politics, for there is no telling how far the evil might extend otherwise. I am not speaking from a partisan standpoint; I am not suggesting anything against this Government or any government. I can quite believe that both parties, perhaps, would be equally guilty of using the pension vote, if it were in any way associated with politics. Therefore it is that I say pensions should be taken out of politics absolutely. The Pension Commission should be appointed in such a way as to make them as independent as the members of the Railway Commission. And my suggestion is that, after the Prime Minister has given us all the information in his possession, a small committee, representing both sides, might sit down, thresh out the matter, anc( make a recommendation to the House.

I am glad to hear from the Prime Minister that the Government intend to deal with this question in a comprehensive way, because, though the war will end sooner or later, it will be a long time before the problems relating to the pensioning of our soldiers will end. I was interested particularly in the remarks of my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) with regard to the treatment of insane soldiers. I gathered that he thought it would be better if these unfortunates were treated in some separate institution. The treatment of the. insane is becoming more and more specialized as scientific knowledge accumulates and the results of different methods of treatment are studied. In all civilized countries the treatment of the insane is engaging the attention of some of the ablest members of the profession to [DOT] which I have the honour to belong. In Canada the insane are treated in asylums or hospitals established and administered by the several provinces. In these hospitals you will find specialists who are studying the vagaries of the insane mind, and applying treatment that brings about wonderful curative results. The question of environment for the insane has been discovered to be very important-perhaps the most important element in their treatment. The insane are given cheery, sunny, comfortable surroundings and congenial company. Specialists are employed to keep the patient's mind occupied and to direct the current of his thoughts in wholesome channels. Another important item is food, and the nursing of these patients is a specialty in itself. Therefore in the majority of cases, you will find our hospitals for the insane in salubrious locations with most favourable surroundings and, those in charge are trained specialists in the care of the insane. There would be great advantages, for the present at any rate, in sending our insane soldiers to *hese hospitals, because of the special cars that they can receive there. As my hon. friend from Edmonton has said, we have had more insanes in this war than in any previous war, because we have had more nerve-racking battles and more nerve-racking experiences in connection with this war than have been known in previous wars. I gather from the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton, that he believes that there is an idea throughout the country that a certain stigma attaches to the individual who has been confined in an insane asylum. Perhaps he is right.

There should be no such stigma, but possibly there is. I understand him to say that for this reason it would be better to have some speeial hospital for the treatment of our insane soldiers. That is a very worthy suggestion. This would mean that we would have a Federal hospital for the insane; a military hospital for the insane, if you will. I assume that at the present time-though I am not sure, for I have not investigated the matter-the insane soldiers are being cared for in the existing asylums of the several provinces. It may be that they have been segregated in these hospitals, possibly in each hospital a military ward has been established, but that, I take it, would not meet the suggestion of my hon. friend from Edmonton. It would ensure for our boys who have come back from the front the attention of highly-trained medical specialists and nurses, but it would not meet the views of the hon. member for Edmonton which is that we should have a separate hospital for our soldiers. That is a suggestion, I think, which is worthy the consideration of the Government. If this war continues, as we have every reason to fear it will, if these awful bombardments go on, as we have every reason to fear they will, there will be an increasing number of insane soldiers returning from the front. I rose merely to support the argument made by the hon. member for Edmonton.
Mr. FRANK S. GLASS (Middlesex East): Like my hon. friend from the Yukon (Mr. Thompson), I noted the remark of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that there might be a stigma attaching to the soldier sent for treatment to one of the existing provincial institutions for the care of the insane. It would be presumption for me to attempt to discuss scientifically, from a medical standpoint the benefit of these institutions in my own province, but I do eay that if the institutions of that kind in the district from which the hon. member for Edmonton comes are anything like those that we have in Ontario, there could be no objection to sending patients to them. In Ontario the word asylum has been almost entirely dropped so far as these institutions are concerned; they are called hospitals (for the insane. If they are all of the character of the one very close to the district in which I live, they might well be called sanitaria for the ihsane. The institution in London, which is supported by the Provincial Government, is one of very long standing. The treatment of patients 105
there is now entirely different from that which prevailed some years ago; medical science, electricity, bath treatments, and so on, have contributed materially to improving the efficiency of the treatment accorded the patients. The percentage of recoveries in these institutions has during the 'last few years been very much larger than ever before. Similar institutions in all parts of the world have adopted improved methods of treatment. I cannot agree, therefore, with my hon. friend when he says that the congregation in one institution of a large number of persons whose mental condition has been disturbed by the war would be as desirable ae their going to the different hospitals of that character that we have throughout the country. These institutions have no longer the character of a prison. The whole surroundings have the character of a sanatorium, of an institution to which one might well go for the recovery of health. Provision is made whereby the patients may indulge in various kinds of sports and amusements; those who may be allowed their liberty have considerable freedom, and, in a sense, may roam about at will. Having regard to the commodious nature of the grounds, the provision for sports and amusements, and the general improvement in methods of treatment at these different institutions, it is reasonable to suppose that more recoveries would be effected by sending the patients to different institutions than by gathering them all into a single hospital. As to the cost of maintaining and treating these patients, I have not the slightest doubt that it would be a privilege and a pleasure to the provinces to take care of our brave boys who have been or may be so afflicted. A great deal can be done for the comfort and happiness of soldiers who have been wounded or incapacitated in various ways, by a system of technical training that will enable them to be useful in some vocation. The man who may have lost an arm may be trained to do something by which he can use his other arm and the rest of his powers in earning a living. I believe that the man who feels that he is, in a measure, contributing to his pwn support is far happier than the man who feels that he is dependent upon the state. Again, if we should deem it necessary to establish a separate institution for those persons whose minds may have been afflicted while at the front, would not the same principle apply to those whose eyesight has been destroyed? I think it is generally agreed that the very best



thing that can be done for those who suffer loss of eyesight is to send them to institutions where for years the care and education of such persons has, under the surveillance of the Government, been carried out according to the ibest methods that science and skill can provide. Much can be done to contribute to a man's happiness in life, even though his sight be gone, and I think that the proper place to take care of such men is in the institution provided especially for that purpose. While I do not know what the needs of the future will be-they may vary according to the number of men who may be so afflicted- it seems to me that for the time being those institutions which for years have specialized in the treatment of subjects of this kind are best fitted to take care of those of our sons who may be so unfortunate as to be afflicted by loss of reason during the course of the war.

I am very glad
indeed to have the assurance of the right hon. Prime Minister that the papers in this matter will be brought down and printed for the information of members of the House, and that the matter will be further taken up in some other form. The. subject is one which is well worthy of careful study. I have endeavoured in a small way to devote attention to the matter, and I am surprised to find that I have arrived at a conclusion different from that of the right hon. gentleman in regard to the comparison between the Canadian and the Australian and English pension lists. There is, of course, difficulty in getting authoritative statements from - England and Australia as to the amounts paid to the different ranks under the different degrees of disablement, in order that comparison can be readily made. Where different degrees are set forth, the matter becomes somewhat complicated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think there was any difference in our views.

There was practically no difference in our views, but my conclusions in regard to the difference between our position and that of Australia were different from those of my right hon. friend. Of course, the right hon. gentleman speaks from authoritative documents which I did not have at hand; I have no doubt that he is correct.
The right hon. gentleman spoke - of the great difference between the amount paid to the English private and that paid to the English colonel, and of the difference existing in that respect between Australia and

Canada. In England this condition is, of course, evidence of the recognition of classes and masses, which we do not have in this country and which do not exist in Australia. We cannot help being struck by the fact that every day Canadian men are going into the ranks who are just as good, socially, intellectually and every other way, as the men who hold command. In fixing the pensions this fact should be recognized, and the wide distinction that exists in England should be totally disregarded here in apportioning pensions to the respective ranks. It is the duty of the Militia Department to see to it that the men who are accepted for service are carefully scrutinized medically before they are allowed to go overseas. It is beyond question that there has been laxity in that respect and that unfit persons have been allowed to go. If you visit any convalescent home to-day you will find some men who should never have gone to the front. The burdens of this country, which we will all assume with the greatest possible feeling of fulfilling our duty, will be sufficiently great in looking after those who were fully competent and fit to go, without having any additional burden imposed upon us by the accepting of men who are not physically fit for service. If there has been any laxity in the past, it is to be hoped that greater care will be taken in the future in the examination of recruits. Then, too, care should be exercised in regard to the age of those who are accepted. You will find men bubbling over with enthusiasm and military ardour who have long passed the age when they can give that vigour and Teal, practical work which is required in this war, because a man may be enthusiastic, but may have a lack of physical vigour which will render him susceptible to conditions which will make him a pensioner more quickly than others. There is no reason for that man going or any man who is not physically fit and strong. The privations in this war are greater than they have been in any other war, and it is better for us to exercise care now than to have to deal with this problem later on.
I have no reason to find any fault with the gentlemen now fulfilling the duties of the Pensions Board; but their duties hitherto have been comparatively light, and have not been at all commensurate with the burdens which will be placed on such a board before the close of the year 1916. I do hope that, both in regard to the board and to the question of the pensions to be paid, before

the close of this session the matter will be put on such a clear, definite, and certain basis that the man going out will know what his rights are,, and that he will feel beyond all question that when he comes home those rights will be recognized, if unfortunately he should fall within the class of people entitled to receive pensions. We will await the bringing down of the papers. I feel assured that the Government, as their views have been stated by the right hon. gentleman, will join with those upon this side of the House in endeavouring to put the question of pensions to be paid to our returning soldiers on the very best possible basis.

Motion agreed to.	"

The House resumed at eight o'clock.

- Mr. E. M. MACDONALD (Pictou) moved:
For a return showing a list of vessels, belonging to the Canadian Government which are on service under the provision of the Canadian Naval Act, and of all vessels not now In service and their present condit'on and suitability for service, and also for a copy of all letters, petitions or communications had by or with the Government in regard to the establishment of a Canadian Naval Brigade.
He said: Mr. Speaker, we are now in the twentieth month of the war, and I am sure that it must have struck every hon. gentleman who ig at all reflective, in relation to our own position, and our position in the Empire, that, while we have heard a great deal about what Canada is doing upon the land, we have heard absolutely nothing about what Canada is doing on the sea, or about what she ought to do on the sea. Whether it is that the hon. gentleman who fills the position of Minister of Militia has, a greater faculty for playing, in the centre of the stage than the hon. gentleman who is Minister of the Naval Service, or whether the lack of aggressiveness of the one accounts for his total abstinence from remark as regards our service on the sea, is a matter upon which I do not purpose to comment particularly. The fact remains that up to date no one has heard of Canada doing anything or attempting to do anything on the sea. This motion which I have submitted to-night is for the purpose of drawing the attention of the House and of the country to the fact that the time has arrived when something ought to be done.
The evening papers contain the announcement that the German fleet is proposing to
come out at last to give battle to the British Navy. It is an object of interest as to what our position in Canada might he if half a dozen or so of German ships succeeded in escaping from the conflict around the north of Scotland, and in making their way across the ocean to our Atlantic seaports. It is an object of interest to inquire what, in that event, our position would be. The situation is that, for the last three months the North Atlantic squadron of the British Navy has been engaged in cruising around in what might be called the South Atlantic, with its headquarters at Jamaica, and has been continually on watch for the purpose of intercepting any vessels which might be engaged in carrying munitions or othefl aid to the Germans and their associates. Like a bolt from the blue there came the announcement about a month ago that two or three German raiders had succeeded in capturing quite a number of British merchant vessels, and that the Appam had succeeded in passing the cordon which is supposed to surround the south Atlantic coast, and found her way into Hampton Roads. Hence it is that the Appam had succeeded in passing the cordon which is supposed to surround the south Atlantic coast, and found her the United States and the ports of Central America. Where is Canada to-day in means for her defence? We might look to Australia. Australia has not only her own defence provided for, hut she is able to send the Sydney and the Melbourne on service, both of these warships having, during the past six or seven months, formed part of the British squadron which is at present in the southern Atlantic. Canada is in this humiliating position, that apparently we have no vessels of any kind, and that, if any German ships made their escape from a conflict in the North Sea, and came across the Atlantic, we would be absolutely defenceless.
It may be said that the information which I ask for should not be brought down because it would indicate our absolutely defenceless position, but with that theory I do not for one moment agree. Where you have a situation which, in the interests of the whole country, requires to he remedied, there is only one way of dealing with it, and that is to face it squarely. No hesitation has been shown in the Imperial Parliament in criticising to the full and in the 'most severe manner the actions both on sea and on land, and the administration in regard to the movement of the forces, and the direction of ships.

Why, only a week ago Winston Churchill left his command in France for the purpose of coming to London to discuss fully and frankly the naval situation, and to point out the imperative necessity of recalling Lord Fisher to the Admiralty. So I have no compunction whatever in bringing up this subject. I say that in the month of January-only two months ago-there was on the Atlantic coast only one vessel belonging to the Department of Naval Service that was fit to go to sea, and that was the very email ship, the Canada, which has only two small guns. There were other vessels attached to the naval service: the Grilse for instance, which is attached to the North Atlantic squadron and in January she was at Bermuda, and is now between Bermuda and Jamaica. Then there was the Stadacona, which was purchased last summer and which has cost this country $104,585 to put in shape. Any one who visited the Halifax dockyard last January could see that she was not in condition to go to sea; in fact, it was freely stated in Halifax that her captain had said she was in euch a condition that he would not venture to put her out to sea. She is only a small vessel, purchased in the United States, and she was never built and never intended for that service. Then there was the Hochelaga, which has cost Canada $92,642; she arrived at Montreal on August 21, and remained there until September 11. She was on duty off the coast from September 11 to December 22, and on February 19-the last date on which I have information regarding her-she was lying in the dockyard. She was therefore not available for any purpose whatsoever from December 22 up to the 19th of February.	Then there was the
Florence, which Sir John Eaton presented to the Naval Service Department. She is a very pretty steam yacht, but any one who faae seen her would realize that she was not intended for our stormy Atlantic coast. She, was not available for winter service at all. Then there was the Tuna, which was being repaired, and is still undergoing repairs. Then there was the Starling, a tug boat; and the Margaret, a small boat; I don't know where she was, but any one who has seen her would realize that she was not fit for Atlantic service. With the exception of the Niobe, these were the only vessels that the Canadian Naval Service had at Halifax in January, 1916. The Niobe was tied up at the wharf, with her guns dismantled, and 
she was being stripped. A house had been built over her for winter, and there was a large number of men going up and down her decks, apparently doing nothing. 1 think about seven hundred men were on board, and apparently they were there without any purpose whatever. So the only vessel we had on the Atlantic coast in January, 1916, was this small vessel the Canada. Is that a proper position for a self-respecting country like Canada to be in? What has Australia done? She adopted a naval policy such as we on this side of the House believe in, she built the Australia, the Sydney, the Melbourne, and other vessels; and she was able not only to protect her own shores, but to send these boats into the Atlantic ocean. The only available boat we had was being dismantled; for what purpose I do not know, and I would like the Minister of the Naval Service to fell us. Going around the coast of Nova Scotia as I did in different vessels and steamers last summer, I met many officers of the British Naval Service, and each and every one of them bore testimony to the value of the Niobe as a first-class vessel in every way. They told the story of how a month after the war began she had her crew on board and was on duty off the coasts of Canada and the United States performing her work just the same as every other vessel that came out from England. But this vessel which was bigger than any of the five vessels that came out and formed the North Atlantic squadron, and which had a heavier armament, was dismantled. That was the situation then, and, as far as I am informed, that is the situation to-day. When any of our transports cross the ocean, certain vessels are detached from the Atlantic squadron, and escort them part way across. Last summer our transports which went from Quebec did not even depend upon these vessels for escort, but were escorted down the gulf of the St. Lawrence to Newfoundland by the Canada and the Grilse. For the last three months, then, and at this moment, with the exception of the British squadron, whose particular duty is off cape Hatteras and along the West India Islands, the only protection Canada has had on the Atlantic coast was the Canada; except for a stray British ship that would come in for coal or supplies. One of the anomalies in this connection is that the ships of the British squadron cannot, or do not, burn coal that is produced on this side of the Atlantic. Day after day you will see in

Halifax harbour half a dozen steam vessels laden with coal, which have been sent out from England with coal supplies for the ships of the squadron. When these warships are not taking in supplies and coal at Halifax, they are off New York or cape Hatteras, or along the West India Islands. It is well that the House should understand the exact situation. If the Minister of Naval Service can inform me that we have any greater protection than I have stated, or can assure the House that our coasts are adequately protected, I shall be very glad to hear from him.
The other portion of my motion calls for:
A copy of all letters, petitions or communications had by or with the Government in regard to the establishment of a Canadian Naval Brigade.
In the Naval Service Act of 1910, there is a provision under which this Government can form a naval reserve, or naval reserves. Provision is also made in the Act for placing men who enlist in these reserves at the service of the Admiralty. In British Columbia a reserve was formed by some enthusiasts who were interested in the protection of Canada from attack by sea, and service in this organization was purely voluntary. I have under my hand the Naval Service reports from 1912 to date, and I cannot find in them anything about the existence of anything like a naval reserve of any kind whatsoever, until I come to the report for 1915, which has been laid on the table of the House during the present session.
I am informed that no official recognition of that purely volunteer naval reserve was given until just before or just after the war broke out. I am informed also that in 1914 Sir Richard McBride communicated with the Premier' of Great Britain, with the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, who was then Secretary of the Admiralty, and with Lord Fisher as to this naval brigade, and as to furnishing recruits from Canada for the British Navy. He received favourable replies from all those sources; but as this Government was not as favourably disposed as was the English Government, no encouragement whatever was given to recruiting, and it was not until after this organization had been in existence for some time that anything was done in the way of recognition. What took place then? It has often been said in this country that you cannot get sailors to serve in the navy. While I speak with some trepidation in regard to the resources of Canada in the presence of gentlemen who come from the central provinces where there are such magnificent resources,
I will not defer in my opinion to those gentlemen in regard to matters affecting ships and those who go down to the sea in ships, because those of us who come from the sea-coast see the conditions there, and know something about fhem. The men who have spoken in this House in days gone by of the impossibility of recruiting men in Canada to serve in the navy have utterly misapprehended the conditions, as is proven by the fact that from this voluntary naval reserve in British iColumbia 200 men are already serving in the British Navy.
Let us see what the public records say as to what can be done in Canada. It will be interesting to hear the explanation of the Minister of Naval Service (Mr. Hazen) as to why he has not attempted to recruit men in Canada for the navy. The necessity of getting men for the navy is quite as great if not greater than getting men for the army. Speaking upon this question in the debate on the Address I read from official sources as to the necessity of recruiting men for the navy. When the English Parliament a few months ago passed the compulsory measure which provided for all men serving under the British flag, they attached an amendment by which the navy on account of its necesities was to have the first right to select from those who were conscripted, and if one studies the English newspapers, one will see that the attempt to get men for the navy is pushed with the greatest possible keenness and energy all through that country. They go to the public schools and get the young men who have never seen an ironclad to serve in the navy, and they recruit in the cities. The necessity at Gallipoli was so great and the conditions in that peninsula so terrible that the older men, who had been reservists and who had retired from the sea, were found manning the great vessels of the Mother Country there. Yet the Minister of Naval Service has never asked the people who lived down by the sea in the Maritime Provinces to rally around the old standard and to proffer their services in fighting England's naval battles. Why has he not done so? I find in the first report which my hon. friend,laid before the House the following statement as to what might be done:
On the arrival of the ships-
The Niobe and the Rainbow.
-at Halifax and Esquimalt respectivly, recruiting was started. By arrangement with the Post Office Department, postmasters were appointed recruiting officers in seventy-five cities and towns in the Dominion; posters were exhibited throughout the Dominion and a recruit-

ing- pamphlet was widely distributed. As a result recruiting has been satisfactory, and the complement of the Niobe is practically complete whilst there are still a few vacancies in the Rainbow. As the advantages of the service become'more widely known, it is anticipated that there will be no difficulty in obtaining recruits.
That was in the year 1912. Then we come to 1913 when my hon. friend laid another report on the table explaining why men were not asked to serve at sea. In that report my hon. friend made himself responsible for this statement:
Owing to the uncertainty of the future naval policy, and the limited accommodation available, no special efforts are being made to obtain redruits for the navy; eligible candidates presenting themselves to the various postmasters detailed as recruiting officers, were sent to the Niobe and the Kaihbow for training, the total number of recruits entered during the year being 126.
