Then my hon. friend, in another part of the report, stated:
Up to the present the fishing population has not been exploited and it is anticipated that recruits can be obtained therefrom who are inured to a sea life and who would find themselves in congenial surroundings in a man of war.
Why was it that the men who lived by the sea were not exploited? Why did the Government not ask the men in the fishing counties of Eastern Canada to serve -in the navy? Beginning with the county of Yarmouth from which our late lamented friend Mr. Law came, and going to the -counties of Queens, Guysborough, Richmond, and Cape Breton, there are thousands of men whose sole occupation from one end of the year to the other is life upon the sea. They have not, with the -same enthusiasm that men from other portions of our country have, offered their services to the Empire on land because the sea is their home, and they have never been asked to serve in the navy. My hon. friend said in 1913:
The fishing population has not been exploited.
Why has it not been exploited if the nation needs men for the navy? Again 1 take my hon. friend's report of 1914:
No recruits have been entered in the ships since October last.
Sometimes we hear about the wonderful pressure in certain departments on account of the war, yet this report indicates that there was no pressure in the Naval Service Department because no recruits have been entered since October last. The report goes on:
H. M. C. S. Niobe Is now in an efficient seagoing condition, her repairs having been completed in December, but on account of deficient

complement, however, the ship is not able to undertake prolonged cruises.
In other words, this first-class cruiser sent out by the British Government and which was declared by this report to be in firstnclass condition in April, 1914, was! according to the report of my hon. friend's own officials, unable to go to -sea because they had not enough men to man her and because they were not endeavouring to get the men. My hon. -friend, in this report of March 31, 1914, further says:
The Government having decided not to continue H.M.C. ships "Niobe" and "Rainbow" in full commission, no recruiting was carried on during the year, and the programme of exercises and training- laid down for these ships was not continued. During the year free discharge was given to those Canadians who entered the service as boys and wished to avail themselves of the offer; in addition, many of the ranks and ratings lent from the Imperial service have completed their engagement under the Canadian Government, and returned to England, without being replaced.
This is the official report of the Department of the Naval Service for the year ending March 31, 1914, and it shows -clearly, as I have already stated, not only that they are not keeping men enough on these vessels to enable them to go to sea, but that no attempt is -being made to get the men.
I have searched these reports carefully, and I can find no reference to the organization of a naval -brigade or reserve. It was not until the latest report was laid on the table of the House this year that the first mention was made of a naval reserve in Vancouver. The reference is as follows: *
The R. N. C. Y. R. chiefly recruited at Esquimau have been actively and usefully employed both ashore and afloat and have shown, both officers and men, commendable zeal in the performance of their duties.
I am aware, however, that from this purely voluntary brigade, which was not recognized until the war began, there have been drafted men now stationed on vessels in the North Atlantic squadron and elsewhere. I am aware of a notice which appeared in a Vancouver newspaper about ten days ago which read:
A recruiting officer will be at room 25 Canada Life building, 640 Hastings street west, Vancouver at 10 a.m. on Monday and Tuesday next, 6th and 7th March, to secure recruits for the Royal Naval (Canadian) Volunteer Reserve stationed at Espnlmalt, B.C., to replace the men of this force discharged recently for "active service" on the Atlantic.
This force, (which was called out on "active service" at the outbreak of war) has now over 250 men serving in ships of the Royal Navy and the Royal Canadian Navy on the Atlantic and

Pacific ocean, besides supplying the guards for H. M. C. dockyards at Halifax, N.S., and Esquimau, B.C., and patrols at these and other points.
Then follows a statement of what is required of recruits.
Now, why is it that the Minister of the Naval Service has not made any attempt on the Atlantic coast to provide for a naval reserve, or a naval brigade, or even to get recruits of some kind? Since the German vessels were driven off the Southern Pacific, there is nothing to menace our western coast. In March, for the first time, the hon. minister asks for recruits, hut in doing so he keeps away from the Atlantic coast. At no time has there been any request for recruits on that coast. Yet, that is where the necessity arises. I do not comment on this with undue severity; I simply call the attention of the House to the fact that we have no protection whatever on the Atlantic coast;-the Niobe is dismantled at the wdiarf, the Canada is the only vessel of any consequence that we have, and she is of very little consequence, and no attempt is made to recruit men for the navy. Yet there is no reason why they should not be recruited. The minister's own reports negative all the arguments put forth elsewhere against recruiting. I would like to know from the Minister of the Naval Service why Canada has no determined to do her part with men on the sea, as she has done with the men on the land.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of the Naval Service):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The resolution of the hon. member for Pictou really relates to two different subjects. The first part is:
For a return showing a list of vessels belonging to the Canadian Government which are on service under the provisions of the Canadian Naval Act, and of all vessels not now in service, and their present condition and suitability for service;
The other part is as follows:
.-and also for a copy of all letters, petitions or communications had by or with the Government in regard to the establishment of a Canadian Naval Brigade.
With regard to this portion, there can be no objection to bringing down all the correspondence. As to the first part about which I have already spoken to my hon. friend, I do -not think it would be in the public interest to give to the world a statement of the Canadian vessels, their present condition and suitability for service, and a general statement of what they are doing. However, the hon. gentleman and I will agree about the matter, and I am confident we shall be able to afford him
all the information he wants. For, listening to my hon. friend, I cannot but think that his resolution is moved, not so much for the purpose of gaining information that would be of value to the country, -as for _ the purpose of making a partisan attack on the Government of the day. This is not the first occasion this session when my hon. friend has referred to this subject. Speaking in the debate on the Address, on the 4th of January last, my hon. friend told of a visit he had made to the navy yard in Halifax on the 2nd of January of this year; and, while he complained that there did not seem to be a great deal of work going on in the navy yard at that time, the principal subject of his complaint was of the way the navy yard was guarded. He said:
Again, here in this dockyard, built by the money of the Imperial Government, which the Imperial vessels use but very rarely and to a very slight extent, anybody who looks honest to the Dominion policeman who stands at the gate of the dockyard can walk in and go anywhere he pleases. I say the Minister of the Naval Service should have that dockyard under the control of men who are there attached to the Niobe.
Later, he said:
There was nobody guarding the dockyard gate except a Dominion policeman. If this Naval Service is not the most awful farce that any Government ever intended to carry through in any country, do you not think that they would have some of their men detailed to guard the gates of this dockyard at the city of Halifax, which is supposed to be the great centre of the Atlantic squadron on this side of the ocean? Yet that was the situation. It seems to me surprising, I am bound to say I was astounded.
He also said:
I bring this matter to the attention of Parliament not from any desire to be partisan in placing the matter before the House ; but I believe that these conditions are such that Parliament should know of them, the Government should be informed of them, and the matter should be dealt with accordingly.
According to the hon. gentleman's .statement, it was the 2nd of January when he visited the dock-yard and was surprised at the lack of activity there. But he did not tell the House that the second day of January was a Sabbath day, nor did he remind the House that it was the day after New Year's Day.

It was not the
Sabbath.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman may have given the wrong date, but the 2nd of January was certainly a Sunday, and the rule of the navy yard is that there shall be no Sunday labour if it can be avoided. The hon. gentleman naturally finds the dock-

yard a quiet spot on Sunday, especially on a Sunday succeeding a holiday so generally observed as New Year's Day. It is hardly fair for the hon. gentleman to represent the condition he found on Sunday as being the ordinary conditions prevailing in this dock-yard. As a-matter of fact, since the war broke out, the dock-yard has been an extremely busy place.
A large number of warships have been based upon Halifax, and the work of repairing these ships and keeping up their supplies, filling vacancies in their crews, providing for their sick and finding accommodation for the crews sent out to recommission them has proved quite a tax on the small staff maintained at the yard. The staff of the Naval Service Department at Halifax has also been obliged to undertake many services in connection- with the war, and to do its share in the defence measures which have been adopted on the Canadian coasts. It is not possible, it is not politic or wise, to describe these measures in d,etail, but the Halifax yard staff has certainly not been idle; it has, not only in our opinion, but in the opinion of the Lords of the Admiralty as well, been doing extremely good work.
That the hon. gentleman was extremely anxious to find, ground for criticism was shown in the remarks that he made about the way in which the dockyard was guarded. The hon. gentleman comes before this House posing as a man who has made a study of naval matters. Will he be surprised when I tell to-im that the measures taken for the protection of the Halifax dockyard are in line with the measures taken for the protection of the dockyards of the Imperial Government? The dockyard was guarded by Dominion policemen. My hon. friend says that is all wrong; that the dockyard ought to be guarded by men taken off the ships, who should be used a^ a patrol in the yard. But, as I say, the systems in force at Halifax and Esquimalt are exactly the same as the systems in force in the yards of the Imperial Government. In those yards it has been found advantageous to have the policing in the hands of a force entirely distinct from the -naval organization, and we have been following that policy in connection with our dockyards on the Atlantic and the Pacific. The outside discipline of the yards is maintained by members of the police force; these men are in a more independent position than men belonging to the ships, who might have a tender feeling with regard to their comrades on shipboard.

It has been found by the Imperial authorities that an independent land force of policemen exercise stricter supervision, and that better results are obtained in this way. The Canadian navy yards have followed the example of the British authorities, and the employment of Dominion policemen as guards in these establishments is giving the most satisfactory results, as is shown from the fact that there has not been the slightest trouble in the yards in Esquimalt or Halifax, from outside interference since the war began. I do not think my hon. friend should complain because the policeman at the gate allowed him to pass. My hon. friend is well known in the province of Nova Scotia; few met are better known. The policemen at the gate knew him; knew that he was a member of Parliament; knew that he was a man who had a right to visit the dockyard if he saw fit; therefore he allowed him access to the yard without challenging his right to enter. Complaints are continually being made by persons who are refused admission to the dockyard-who are stopped by the policeman when they attempt to enter. They claim that the policeman ought to have known who they were and should have allowed them to enter without having a pass from the proper authorities. This is an indication of the fact that in moving for those papers my hon. friend is desirous of making political capital, of making a little picayune criticism. His chief criticism in this connection is that the naval authorities of Canada are pursuing exactly the -same course so far ais guarding the dockyards is concerned as is followed in the Imperial dockyards of the United Kingdom.
My hon. friend has sought to attack the Government by saying that Canada has no defence upon the Atlantic or upon the Pacific coasts. If Canada has no defence; if we are not contributing as much as we should to the splendid defence that is .given to us by the British Navy to-day, I ask this House and this country, whose fault is it? In view of the way my hon. friend and the members of his party in 1913, by every method known to parliamentarians, obstructed the passage through this House of a Bill designed for the purpose of giving assistance to the Navy in the Mother Country; in view of the emergency that was then threatening us; in view of the cloud that was then hanging over our heads; in view of the fact that my hon. friend's party induced their partisan majority in the Senate t6 throw out the Bill providing for

the building of three of the largest ships of war that science could devise and that money could buy-in view of these facts, I ask my hon. friend if it is not a matter of courage on his part to attack this Administration because Canada is not in a better position to defend her coast to-day, and because she has to rely, as she has in the past, upon the protection of the British Navy? Previous to the elections of 1911 the hon. gentleman's party made a certain pretence of naval defence in this country. They asked for tenders for certain cruisers and torpedo boat destroyers. Tenders were received, but they were put in a pigeon-hole, kept there for about six months, and did not see the light of day again until after the present administration came into power. If hon. gentlemen opposite were honest in their desire at that time to strengthen our naval defences, how was it that the contracts for the construction of Ihese ships were not awarded? Was it, as appears to be the case, that they wanted to play politics with these ships at the coming election, and to make the people of Montreal, St. John, Halifax and Cape Breton believe that it was the intention of the then Government to construct a Canadian navy, and that the ships would be built at each of these places? The hon. member for St. John time and again has suggested that if the contracts had been awarded by the late Government, these ships would have been built at St. John; yet the right hon. leader of the Opposition told this House in most emphatic language that had the contracts been entered into, these ships would, at the time that he was speaking, be under constru'ction at the city of Montreal. Everybody who knows anything about the election of 1911 knows that these statements were allowed to play a considerable part in the attempt of hon. gentlemen opposite to obtain support for the party then in power in the constituency of Halifax and the constituencies of Gape Breton. Did the hon. gentlemen neglect to award the contract for these ships, the tenders for which they had had in their possession months before the general election, simply because they were playing the game of politics with the whole nival question? When we came into power, and when these tenders were taken out of the musty pigeon holes in which they had been allowed, to remain for months, indicating the absolute lack, of sincerity on the part of my hon. friend and the party opposite in regard to this matter, we found awaiting us reports from Commander Roper and Admiral Kings-mill stating that to proceed with the construction of these vessels would be a mistake; that when completed they would have passed their time and would have to be included with those vessels that were obsolete or in a state of obsolescence. These are the facts with regard to the action of my hon. friend opposite.
What was the action of the Consgrvative party in regard to the matter? The present Prime Minister, then leader of the Opposition, told this House and told this country that if he were returned to power he would consult with the Admiralty as to what was the best thing to be done with a view to assisting the navy of the Empire in the event of war being declared. After the right hon. gentleman came into power, in the year 1912, he, with certain of his colleagues, went to Great Britain, and there had consultation with the Prime Minister, Mr. Asquith, with the Lords of the Admiralty and with other naval authorities, as to what was the best thing that Canada could do to assist the British navy in the event of war taking place. After my hon. friend came back to Canada, at the next session of the House in 1913, he laid upon ithe table , of the House a state document received from the Lords of the Admiralty, which, after reviewing the situation-showing to any man who could read between the lines -that an emergency was apprehended, that war was to be feared-concluded in these words:
The Prime Minister of the Dominion having: inquired in what form any immediate aid that Canada might give would be most effective, we have no hesitation in answering, after a prolonged consideration of all the circumstances, that it is desirable that such aid should include the provision of a certain number of the largest and strongest ships of war which science can build or which money can supply.
And, acting upon the advice of the Admiralty, my right hon. friend, with the concurrence of the Government of which he was leader and of the party which supported him in this House, introduced a Bill to provide for the construction of three capital vessels in accordance with the recommendations of the Admiralty. We believed then and we believe now that the Admiralty were the best judges of what was required for Empire defence under the circumstances that then existed. When my right hon. friend placed his proposals before Parliament, they were met with every possible ridicule, they were met with every possible method of obstruction that parliamentary skill in obstruction could devise. We were

told that there was no emergency. The idea of war then or in the near future was ridiculed, laughed to scorn, by the hon. members on the opposite side of the House. They, not content with ridiculing the idea that there was danger of war, that there was any war cloud hanging over the Empire, that there was any emergency that would have to*be met; they were not content with making these utterances in the House, but when the resolution had been carried in this House they followed it into the other House and got their partisan majority in the Senate to throw out that measure designed for the protection of the British Empire. So, if my hon. friend wants to know why Canada was not better prepared for the [DOT]defence of the -seas, why -she was not contributing .more to the British Empire, I advise him to go and consult his friends in the Senate who, at the suggestion <md dictation of the members of his party in this House, threw out the Bill designed and intended for that purpose. But my hon. friends were not content with the attacks which they had made in Parliament upon this proposal; they followed ' it up in the literature which they issued to the people of this country. No emergency, they said; they laughed at the idea of an emergency. The idea of war with Germany was the most impossible thing, and the right hon. gentleman who leads the party on the opposite side took the occasion in one of his speeches to point out what a -splendid man the German Emperor was and how -he might be relied upon to maintain peace under all circumstances. Hon. gentlemen then, as to-day, flooded this country with pamphlets for partisan purposes. I hold in my hand a pamphlet issued by the Central Information Office of the Canadian Liberal party in Ottawa in 1913, known as publication number 6. It is entitled "Is there an emergency, conflict otf opinions examined in the light of the facte." And this pamphlet of 24 pages is devoted to - 9 P-m. argument to the effect that there was no more arrant nonsense in the world than for any body of men to contend that there was any danger of wa; be tween Great Britain and Gerrnany, and that the idea of an emergency was simply the purest sort of nonsense, the result of the imagination of people who were anxious to stir up strife in the country, and that there was not the slightest foundation in fact for it. And yet, scarcely 12 months after this publication was written, the world was at war, the Empire was engaged 
in a fight for its very existence, which has been continuing ever since and which may, unfortunately, continue for many months to come. Let me quote a few passages from this pamphlet. I find on page 5:
Here then is the difference between -Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Borden. Sir Wilfrid Laurier denies that there is an emergency. Mr. Borden will not say that there is an emergency, but to avoid bringing down a permanent policy, either the same as or different from that to which Parliament unanimously agreed, has thought it necessary to make it appear that an emergency exists and that Canada should present to Great Britain the three largest ships of war in the world at a cost of $35,000,000, and then work out a permanent policy. Who is right?
Is there a man in Canada to-day who will not say that the right hon the leader of the Government was right and foresaw what was going to happen in hie policy of desiring to have three capital ships of war, even if they had cost $35,000,000 or more, so that when war came those ships, flying the flag of Canada, might be found on the -seas, -protecting not only Canadian commerce, but the commerce of other parts of the Empire as well, was right, and that the right hon. gentleman was taking a proper course and one which every patriotic man in this country now regrets was not followed, so that Canada might have taken a more active part in the .defence not only of this country but of the Empire -than it is able to take to-day, owing to the unfortunate and unpatriotic attitude taken by hjn. gentlemen opposite on that occasion. -But, Sir, this pamphlet goes on for page after page to support this contention. I find this paragraph on page 8:
The relative strength of British and German fleets is evidence of no emergency, since the supposed emergency is in referenec to Germany. What is the rel-ative strength of the German and British fleets? Here is the statement of the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, First Lord of the Admiralty, given in the House of Commons at Westminster, on Monday, July 22, 1912, in the course of an explanation of the scope and character of the new German navy law and its effect.
Then, th-ey quote Mr. Churchill's words, concluding as follows :
I hope it will be sufficient for me to say that the -arrangements proposed will, in the opinion of the Admiralty, be adequate for the needs of 1S-14 and 1915.
Then, the editor of his pamphlet, issued from the bureau of the Canadian Liberal Party at Ottawa, goes on to say:
In the face of such a statement as this, how can Mr. Borden and his followers, with any pretense of justification, contend that there is

an emergency at the present time, or even a likelihood of one in the immediate future? Elsewhere in the same speech Mr. Churchill refers to what could be done " at any time when the Admiralty consider that there is an emergency,'' clearly indicating that the Admiralty has no belief in any emergency at the present time.
Not only did they argue that there was no emergency, but they argued that Mr. Winston Churchill and the Lords of the Admiralty had no belief in the existence of any emergency at that time. They go on and quote declarations by -responsible ministers to prove the non-existence of an emergency in face of the fact that those same responsible ministers or Lords of the Admiralty informed this House and this country that it was desirable that any aid Canada should give and the- aid that would be most effective would include the provision of a -certain number of the largest and strongest ships of war which science could build or money could supply. But they were not content with issuing one pamphlet on the subject to -show that there was no emergency; they issued a -second pamphlet from which I wish to read a few quotations. It was published in 1913, and was also issued from the central information office of the Canadian Liberal Party at Ottawa, on the memorandum prepared by the Board of Admiralty on the general naval situation. In it they proceeded to criticise the statement prepared by the Admiralty and said:
There is therefore nothing in the memorandum with respect to the German situation which has not already been given to the British public and the world, and which was not -before the British Parliament at the time the Naval estimates were under discussion and Mr. Borden and his colleagues were in England. With these facts before them the British Government saw no existence of an emergency.
Why, therefore, should the Canadian Government draw inference of any such existing? The statement of British ministers in the debates when those facts were laid before the British Parliament are significant, and should be read in Canada when considering the inference to be drawn from the memorandum.
Again it stated:
Could any policy be given under these circumstances than that suggested by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in his reply to Mr. Borden? Referring to the Admiralty Memorandum Sir Wilfrid said:
This document shows that there is no emergency, that England is in no danger whether Imminent or prospective. But the document discloses a condition of things, of which, indeed, we knew, but upon which has now been placed the sanction of official correspondence.
Therefore I say that my hon. friend from Pictou, and hon. gentlemen of the party to
which he belongs, have not read that memorandum from the Admiralty. Having had the assurance given to this House by the Prime Minister, after consultation with the Lords of the Admiralty and with the naval authorities and the Government of Great Britain, that, from the information imparted to the House and from other information which he could not impart, the condition of affairs was such that there was need for strengthening the (British navy in view of the emergency which, it was believed, was coming; with these facts before the House, hon. gentlemen opposite declined to believe that there was any emergency, declined to believe that there was any danger of a war in Europe, declined to believe that the institutions of the British Empire and of Canada were at stake, or were in danger in the prospective future, to quote the language of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) opposite; they refused to accept any of these statements, obstructed the Bill in its passage through this House, and then got their partisan majority in the Senate to reject it when it went to Upper Chamber. Therefore, I say to my hon. friend from Pictou that when he asks why this country is not doing her duty in the matter of defence upon the seas, I say: ask your leader and your party, and ask the Liberal majority in the Senate. That is the answer I give.

My hon. friend had better ask Mr. Bourassa.
Mr. HAZE'N:	My hon. friend from Pictou need not get cross; he need not display temper in regard to this matter, and talk about asking Mr. Bourassa. My hon. friend asked a question, and I am giving him the answer, which is the answer that nine-tenths of the people of this country would give. The people of this country, who are not blinded by partisan considerations will, I venture to say, declare that it is the correct answer to the question asked in this House to-night by the hon. member.
My hon. friend from Pictou has gone further. He has said:	why has not the
Government of Canada enlisted men to form a naval brigade, to go over to assist the navy on the other side of the ocean. While-I have a very great regard for the learning and ability of my hon. friend, I am disposed to think that he does not understand what the purposes and duties of the naval brigade have been in the present war, or what part they have served. Perhaps my hon. friend will be astonished to learn that the naval brigade on the other

side is formed of the surplus of men available after the ships 'of the navy have been manned. When war broke out, they were formed into regiments, and fought in the trenches, at Antwerp and in other parts, just as the men enlisted for military service fought. In not enlisting men to form a naval brigade we acted not on our own judgment, but on the jugment of the British authorities. I would ask my hon. friend whether, if these men were going to serve in the trenches, at Antwerp, and other places, as the soldiers have served, there was any reason for having two different bodies organized for the same service, one under the Militia Department and Jthe other under the Naval Department.
Does my hon. friend say that Great Britain did not require any recruits for her navy?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I say that at the time when war broke out, Great Britain not only did not require any recruits for her navy, but she had about 20,000 men enlisted for naval purposes who were not required to serve in the navy, and who were formed into naval brigades to fight just as the soldiers fight at the front. When war broke out, or soon afterwards, a statement was issued by Mr. Graham Green, the permanent Secretary of the Admiralty, relating to the formation of a Koyal Naval Division. Our attention was called to this, and on September 22, the department called for information as to the formation of a Naval Brigade. On September 25 the information was forwarded to us, with a statement that the list of candidates for commissions was closed, and that no further officers were required. It said nothing whatever about the necessity of enlisting men for the ranks.
The Press Bureau published a statement which was signed by Mr. Winston Churchill, then First Lord of the Admiralty, and part of which I will read to the House to show the correctness of the statement I have made. On September 6 the Press Bureau published the following statement:
The Press Bureau has received the following communication from the Secretary of the Admiralty :
After providing for all present and foreseeable future needs of the fleets at sea, there remained available a large number of men belonging to the Royal Marines, Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve, Royal Fleet Reserve, and Royal Naval Reserve. A portion of these have been organized into one marine and two naval brigades, the whole comprising the infantry of one division, to be called the Royal Naval Division. The marine brigade, for the organization of which all preparation had been made before the war, has been for some time in being at a strength of 3,000, and has already been employed at
I .Mr. Hazen.l
active service at Ostend. The two naval bri-gades have been organized in the first instance at a strength of 3,750 each, and have been in camp since August 19. The cadres of their eight battalions have been formed from the Royal Naval Reserve men forming on these as they were despatched from the ports. The three brigades were fully constituted by the 24th August and entered at once upon a period of field training to fit them for service ab:oad if required in the New Year.
Just as the military are trained in the camps for service abroad, not for service on the sea.
In the meanwhile they will be organized and trained under the Admiralty and will remain available for service afloat should any unexpected needs arise.
There follows a statement as to how they would be made up, into different regiments and brigades. Then it says:.
The Royal, Naval Division will be completely equipped in all respects by the Admiralty with field hospitals, transport, ammunition column, signal companies, cyclists, motor cars, and machine guns. An aeroplane squadron from the Naval Wing, complete with transport, etc., will be available when required. If at any time the naval situation becomes sufficiently favourable to enable this force to be definitely released by the Admiralty for military duty, it will be handed over intact to the Army for general service. The training, discipline, experience and quality which the personnel already possess should, after five or six months' special instruction in field duties, enable units of high quality to be produced.
And so on, showing distinctly that the surplus of men that they had after manning the ships and providing for the Naval Service, was being formed into a naval brigade to be trained in the field for field service, and to perform, as they have performed since'the war broke out, exactly the same services which the military have performed in the trenches, at Antwerp, and [DOT]other places on the Continent.
I now wish to submit to the House a memorandum on the subject, showing in *plainer language exactly what that means:
At the beginning of the war the Admiralty called out the Royal Naval reservists, composed of men engaged in Mercantile marine but trained to a certain extent in the Royal Navy.
When these men responded to the call the Admiralty found themselves with a large body of trained seamen, from which they manned the ships ready to put to sea and still had a considerable number of men over. To utilize the services of these keen eager men, a Naval Brigade was organized, and at the same time the inrush of Naval Reserve men was checked, and instructions were received in Canada that only men specially needed by the Admiralty should be sent forward. The Naval Brigade thus organized, while formed of reserved seamen, was partly officered by Naval Officers and partly by Army Officers. The men were trained as a military unit, given the uniform of the land force, were armed and equipped in exactly the same day as the infantry regiments, and

took their places in the trenches alongside of the latter. The exploits of this Naval Brigade have heen noted at Antwerp and elsewhere; they have served as infantry regiments throughout the war. The only hold retained on them by the Admiralty was that these men having received preliminary training as seamen, should he available for service on Shipboard when required.
The organization of this Naval Brigade is, therefore, exactly similar to that of the land regiments, and there would be absolutely no reason for Canada organizing two different systems of forces. There does not exist in this country a sufficient number of naval officers to undertake the training of naval regiments, and it seemed far wiser to enlist all the willing men under the army organization, instead of duplicating that organization and administering part of it under the Militia Department, and part under the Department of the Naval Service. This would mean added expenditure without any increase in efficiency. The Canadian Government therefore, decided that no possible object would be gained by dividing their organization, and advised the few men who wished to enlist in Naval Brigades to enlist in Overseas Forces.
At the beginning of the war a number of Boyal Naval reservists residing in Canada left for England to join the forces at their various headquarters, but this movement was stopped by the Admiralty as they felt they had a sufficient number of men on hand. The men who went from Newfoundland were men belonging to the Royal Naval Reserve who had been already trained in the Royal Navy, which maintains a training station at St. Johns. I
I therefore ask .my hon. friend what object would have been served in organizing a naval brigade, and giving it exactly the same training as wae given to the men organized in the militia regiments, and then sending them across the seas to do exactly the same work and stand side by side in the trenches with the overseas military forces? Would it have l|een prudent to divide our forces? Would it have been economiea'l? Would it have made for greater efficiency? No, Sir, it was far better to have all the men organized under one department. That was the course we decided upon after conference and consultation with the British army and naval .authorities.
On August 2, having received a notice that the Admiralty had called out the Royal Naval Reserves we gave notice from the Naval Department to that effect to all the collectors of customs in Canada, and asked them to arrange wide publication ashore and afloat. I have here a copy of the telegram sent to the collector of customs at Sydney, N.S., on August 2:
Admiralty have called out Royal Naval Reserve. Please arrange wide publication ashore and afloat.
Naval.
On the 7th of August we wired to Admiral Kingsmill, who was in Toronto:
Public advertisement is being inserted in papers that R.N.R. men desiring information as to transportation .should apply direct to Naval Service Department, Ottawa. They are then being informed to apply to station agent at their respective towns, presenting their papers and telegrams. Arrangements are being made with the Canadian Pacific railway, Canadian Northern railway, Grand Trunk railway, and Intercolonial railway passenger officers to authorize the ncessary transportation on adoption of this procedure.
Naval.
On the 18th of August we received this despatch from the Admiralty:
London, August 18, 1914.
Naval, Ottawa.
R. N. R. officers, seamen, stokers, not to be called out unless services required locally.
(Signed) Admiralty.
Which showed that the British Admiralty had more men than they required for the manning of their ships. Shortly after the outbreak of war, members of the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve offered to proceed to England to join the Royal Naval Brigade which had been formed there. The number available was 120 men and 9 officers.
In view of the length of training which the Naval Brigade in England had already had (over two months), and the necessity for the services of the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve men in British Columbia; in view also of the absence of all officers on active naval service, who were qualified to train the applicants sufficiently, and finally on account of the inadvisability of sending totally untrained men to England for service in the Naval Brigade, it was decided not to grant the request of the members of the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve. As the Naval Brigade is recruited for service ashore, and as applicants for entry in Canada could perform equally good service with the overseas forces recruited under the Militia Department, applicants were advised to enlist with the Canadian Overseas forces.
An offer under date of November 8, 1915, was received to recruit a " Special Pioneer and Water Transportation Corps " to consist of 200 men comprising four units, from Mr. P. E. Scharschmidt. This was submitted to the Department of Militia, and thence to this department by Hon. Sir Richard McBride, Premier of British Columbia. This corps was not considered by the Department to he of a naval character.
A further submission from Mr. R. H. Swenerton for the formation of a battalion

among naval volunteers for overseas military service to be given naval training, but later to be attached to the Expeditionary Forces, was given consideration. It was considered that time and expenditure would be saved if these men were to enlist with the battalions being recruited for active service.
Suggestions for the formation of a naval brigade in Nova Scotia were forwarded from Mr. Charles Archibald to the Prime Minister, and thence to this department. Mr. Archibald's suggestions were considered, but the same objections which the department met in other cases obtained. The Admiralty were, however, on a later date, requested to inform this department if they required recruits from Canada for service in the navy, to be trained in the Imperial Navy. No reply has been received from the Admiralty, and the question is therefore being held in abeyance.
What date is that?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Some time in the last few months. Had the British Admiralty evinced the slightest desire that we should send men from this country for the purpose of serving in the British Navy, or had they, in response to our inquiry, intimated that they would like us to send men forward to assist them in their naval warfare, we would have been desirous to organize, to the best of our ability, forces for that purpose. Not only was no such information given, not only was no such request .made, but, on the contrary, the documents which I have read to the House show that the British authorities had more men for the naval service than they actually required, and the despatch sent us in August, 1914, showed that they did not want us to call out the naval reserve men in this country to act as stokers, etc., in view of the large number of men in the Old Country available for the naval service. I think I may leave that question as it is at the present moment, and I think my hon. friend, when he charged us with not doing our duty in this matter, really did not understand the functions and duties of a naval brigade. Had the hon. gentleman understood that the naval brigade in Great Britain was the surplus of men organized after the navy had 'been fully manned, after all the ships ready for sea had been called out; had he understood that those men were formed into battalions, that they were drilled as the militia are
TMr. Hazen/I
drilled and that they fought side by side with the militia regiments-the only difference being that they were available to be called upon should their services be required for the navy-had my hon. friend comprehended all that, I do not think he would have made this attack on the Naval' Department.
My hon. friend has referred to the vessels that we have at present in the naval service of the Dominion. In a few minutes I will give the House a very full statement, without going into details which should not be made public, of the work that the Naval Department has done since the outbreak of the war, and I think the hon. gentleman will see that his attack is neither well justified nor well founded. The hon. gentleman says that we to-day have no means of defence. To-day not a single troopship has, while crossing from Canada to the Mother Land, met with disaster although troopships have been going and ships have been coming ever since the thirty ships with over 30,000 men from Valcartier, the greatest armada that ever crossed the water, sailed from Quebec. Ever since our troops have been going until at the present date over
100,000	Canadian troops have been sent across the water, and there has not been a single disaster, nor a single casualty. During the same period the trade routes across the sea have been maintained in safety and not a single Canadian vessel carrying munitions of war, or goods for the British Government or for any of the Allied Governments, has up to the present met with misfortune, because we have had the protection of that navy which alone stands between us and disaster, a navy to which we have never contributed a single dollar and which the hon. gentlemen opposite prevented us from contributing to most substantially in 1913.
Does my hon. friend think that, if we had sent that money over, Canada would have been in a better position than Australia is?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If we had equipped those
three capital ships of war, we would have been doing what the British Admiralty, the best authority on the question, said was the most effective way of assisting in the naval service of the Empire. My hon. friend has gone out of his way to attack what we have done. While we have not been able to do very much in the way of actual defensive operations-

Hear, hear.
' Mr. HAZEN:-we could have done a great deal in the way of defensive and offensive operations if we had had those three capital ships of war; and more than that, my hon. friends opposite, when they were in power, might have done something if they had not held up their tenders for six months in erder, in the elections of 1911, to get the votes of people in certain localities by making them believe that each of those localities would be the place where the ships would be built when the contracts were finally entered into. My hon. friend opposite says that we are doing nothing; that we have only had vessels for patrol work and mine sweeping purposes. All that work has been entered upon by the Naval Department after careful consultation with the authorities of the Admiralty, with their full approval and in some cases at their request.
My hon. friend has referred to the Niobe, and he says that we have laid her up in Halifax harbour, and that she is dismantled. I will give the House the facts with regard to the Niobe and I do not think any public interest at the present time will suffer by my doing so. The Niobe was completed in 1897, and is, therefore, some eighteen years old, which in these days is a very respectable age for a warship. She was purchased by Canada in 1910, and was used as a training ship on the Halifax station. It was found difficult to keep the crew of the Niobe up to full strength, and in 1913 it was decided to reduce the crew and most of the ratings lent by the Admiralty to the Canadian Government returned to England. In the spring of 1914, when the Rainbow was commissioned for service in Behring sea, most of the Canadian ratings still on the Niobe were utilized to make up the complement of the Rainbow, and, therefore, at the opening of the war only a very few men were on the ship. A crew was enlisted made up from the Imperial ratings from the Shearwater and the Algerine, which were laid up at
- Esquimalt, from .a few Canadian ratings, from a number of ex-naval ratings residing in Canada who were enlisted, as volunteers for the war, and from Royal Naval Reserve ratings from Newfoundland.
In the spring of 1915, the Niobe, having been at sea and in continuous service for some nine months, began to show signs of wear in her machinery. It was reported that the funnels would need renewing at an early date. On examination of the machinery it was found that the boilers would very soon be in need of very large repairs, ^.nd, as the vessel .had been due for a gem eral refit for some time, it was realized that it would be necessary to lay the vessel up for a long period of time, and spend a large sum of money on repairs and refit.
It would have been necessary to have this refit made in the Imperial dockyards, which, at this time, are filled with more important work. It was considered that it would not be advisable to spend this money or devote so much time to repairing a ship which would be of little value as a fighting unit. On the other hand, it was necessary to provide at Halifax a depot for the many Imperial ratings who are continually passing through this station, and it was a matter of convenience to have a ship in which the various auxiliary services centred at Halifax could be accommodated. It was, therefore, decided to lay the ship up with a nucleus crew sufficient to keep the ship in proper condition, and with a staff of men sufficient to provide for the transient ratings. This was done after consultation with the Admiralty and with its approval.
While the number of men and officers at present entered on the books of the Niobe is about 800, only 337 of these are attached to the service of the ship; the other men compose the crews- of various auxiliary ships or are engaged in the various auxiliary services at Halifax, St. John, Sydney, or elsewhere, and are borne on the books of the Niobe for purposes of discipline and of accounting. During the month of November some 450 Imperial ratings were accommodated on the Niobe. The vessel is, therefore, discharging her duties as a depot ship, and is being made useful within the limits of her present capacity. And that, at the present time, is about all she is fit for. It would not be wise policy, in view of the fact that the shipyards of Great Britain are crowded with important work, to send her across for repairs, to wait the months required to repair her, and spend the enormous sums of money necessary in order to put her in shape to enable her to go to sea again in connection with the purposes of active naval warfare.
The hon. member has referred to the Hochelaga and the Stadacona, bought last year by the Naval Department for patrol work in the gulf of St. Lawrence. These vessels have discharged most admirably the work for which they were intended. Certain repairs have had to be placed upon

them, as is the case with all vessels; but the experts of the Naval Department, on whose advice they were purchased and whose reports were submitted to me before I authorized the purchase, are thoroughly satisfied that they have done their work well, that they are good boats for the work for which they were purchased, and that they will do good work for another summer and probably to the end of the war. The statement that the captain of one of these vessels refused to go to sea in his vessel, is, as far as our department knows, an absolute misrepresentation. There is no foundation for it in fact, and not the slightest justification for any one making the statement made by my hon. friend from Pictou.
Since the war broke out the Naval Department has done a great deal of work in connection with other matters. Certain men were sent by us to England, and of these I will give a brief statement
All officers on the retired, resigned and emergency lists, with certain specified exceptions, were sent to Great Britain, their number being estimated at 50.
A considerable number of Royal Fleet Reserve, Royal Naval Reserve, and prisoner ratings, and ex-naval ratings, other than the above (i.e., men who had taken discharge at the end of the first period oi 12 years' service, who had bought their discharge, etc.). There is no means of ascertaining their number, even approximately, but it probably amounts to several hundreds and may possibly have exceeded 1,000.
Two hundred officers for the Royal Naval Air Service all entered in Canada. Up to the present time, 176 have been sent to Englhnd, and are engaged in the Air Service of Great Britain, bringing credit to Canada, and doing their work well, so far as we know.
As many engine-room artificers and electrical artificers as could be obtained after considerable press publicity were obtained, and only twenty of that class of men were willing to go.
We have been asked to have lists made of the men willing to serve in the Royal Naval Reserve Motor Boat Patrol. We. called for applications, and several hundred applications have been received up to the present time. We are informed by the Admiralty, who asked us to prepare a list of these men, that an officer is coming to Canada to look over the men who have applied, to examine them for their fitness and make selections from their number. In the

Naval Department, we have had a great deal to do in connection with the transportation of munitions and goods for the British Government and the Allied Governments. At the present time there are seventy-five transports on the Atlantic, which are sailing under instructions from us. Between July and November fifty ships, not including timber ships, sailed from Montreal, and were given sailing orders from us. Since November 30, up to March 13, thirty-six store ships have sailed from St. John and twenty-nine from Halifax. The sailings for the near future will be two or three a week from the port of Halifax, and four or five a week from the port of St. John.
In the store and contract branch, the department has been very busy, carrying on work, not only for ourselves but for the British Navy and the navies of the Allied nations. This work has been carried on at the dockyards at Halifax and Esqui-malt, and elsewhere as required. 'Contracts for naval stores entered into to date exceed $1,000,000 in value, and cover a very large	variety of	material,
including provisions, clothing, naval stores of all kinds, ordnance and torpedo stores, fuel, etc. Contracts have been made on both coasts to provide supplies of fresh provisions at a moment's notice for Canadian and Imperial ships. In addition to supplies for the Canadian services, large quantities of provisions, clothing, and naval stores have been supplied from stock at the dockyards and by direct purchase to Imperial ships, and also to His Majesty's dockyard in Bermuda. The value of stock held at the dockyards has averaged well over $600,000, and the total issues, not including fuel or fresh provisions, are about three-quarters of a million to date. Supplies, not including fuel, have been made to the Admiralty for various services, including His Majesty's ships and Bermuda dockyards, to the value of approximately $200,000; to the Japanese Government to the value of approximately $30,000, and smaller quantities to the French and Russian Governments and ships of the Royal Australian Navy. Very large quantities of coal have been handled both at Halifax and at Esquimalt, amounting in the case of- Halifax to approximately 150,000 tons, and in the case of Esquimalt to about 40,000 tons. Charters have been entered into with the owners of 18 vessels on the Atlantic coast for various services, including mine-sweeping, patrol and examination services and harbour defence services. In addition 14 large motor launches have been chartered

for patrol service in the gulf of St. Lawrence and on the Atlantic coast, and five for similar work on the Pacific coast. Supply depots have been arranged as necessary at convenient points on the coast for the use of patrol vessels. The arrangements entered into with the Admiralty and the acting Director Overseas Transport have been continued in force and considerably enlarged. There are now in the Canadian transport service about 75 fine modern ships carrying supplies. Up to the close of navigation at Montreal over 300,000 tons of freight had been handled by this service, and the monthly tonnage exported will reach, it is expected, 150,000 tons per month in the near future. In the month of February alone, at the ports of Halifax and St. John, 138,000 tons of freight was shipped. The Canadian Transport Service is maintained on the following basis:	The Admiralty supply the necessary tonnage and advise the department from time to time of contracts entered into for delivery at [DOT]Canadian ports by the Imperial Government.
This department is a medium of communication in all matters affecting the service. The acting Director of Overseas Transport has immediate charge of the organization of the loading of the ships, and the arrangements by which the material reaches the seaboard. He reports to the department the cargoes loading in each ship, which are in turn communicated to the Admiralty. These arrangements have worked smoothly and without friction. There has been little or no delay occasioned any of the ships. Contracts for coal have been maintained on favourable terms and up to December 31st, coal to the extent of over $400,000, had. been purchased on behalf of this service in Canada.
In addition to the export work of the Transport Service, this department has arranged for the shipment of over forty cargoes of timber, aggregating about 125,000,000 feet, from the ports of Quebec, Gaspe, Chatham, St. John, Halifax, and from British Columbia ports, to European ports on 'behalf of the Imperial Government. And whereas, at one time, it was feared that it would be impossible to obtain tonnage enough to carry across the sea the munitions of war and goods required-hay, oats, and other products of Canada-that idea has been absolutely dispersed. There have been plenty of transports during the winter for these purposes, and they have 106
been able to handle all the cargoes that the railways have been able to deliver for them at the different ports. I am sorry to have to inform the House that last night a vessel at St. John that was loaded with a cargo for Australia was burned. There were no munitions of war in the cargo and no goods for the Allies. The vessel was loaded with motor cars, carbide, paper, and other articles of commercial value. The fire which broke out some time early Sunday was supposed to have been absolutely extinguished, but early this morning an explosion occurred in the ves* sel, with the result that the captain was killed and the vessel sank to the bottom of the water at the face of the dock. I understand that the explosion was caused by the water that was poured into the vessel for the purpose of extinguishing the. flames coming into contact with the carbide. This generated gases and caused the explosion. While the loss of life and the loss of the vessel and its cargo are unfortunate, one of the most unfortunate results is that for the rest of the season the dock, which was sorely needed for the loading of vessels to go across the seas, will be practically useless. The dock is controlled, I believe, by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The difficulty will be to remove the vessel before navigation opens on the St. Lawrence in order that vessels may lay at the dock and receive cargoes. The occurrence is one which is very much regretted, particularly at the present time. No injury was done to the dock or to the sheds upon it; all injury was confined to the vessel itself.

Will the minister kindly state to the House the rates of freight for merchandise which is carried upon vessels under the control of the Admiralty? How do the rates compare with what they were before the war broke out?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As I understand the matter, the goods to be loaded on these transports are delivered at the dock; they are then carried across the ocean for the British Government. I do not think that the rate of freight is an important consideration, because it is paid by the British Government in respect of all munitions of war and other goods sent across the water. I am speaking of transports carrying munitions of war, of which there are seventy-five, and all goods required [DOT]foT the British Government and for the Allies for the purposes of the war.
Do I understand that all these vessels which are under the control of the Naval Service, are owned by the British Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are not owned by the British Government, but they have been requisitioned or commandeered by the British Government for this purpose. Vessels belonging to our own people in Canada have been requisitioned; vessels owned by companies in St. John and by the Dominion Coal Company have been requisitioned. Vessels owned all over the country, not only in Canada, but in other parts of the Empire, have been requisitioned for similar purposes.
You have nothing to do with the rate of freight?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. There are vessels, too, for carrying lumber requisitioned by the British Government. I understand that in New Brunswick there is a great deal of lumber on the wharves that has actually been paid for, but which has not yet gone overseas. In due course that will be sent for and taken away. Lumber will be sent from Chatham, and from other north shore ports. During the winter large quantities of lumber are sent from St. John and Halifax for the British Government. The lumber is sold to be delivered on this side of the water-payable on delivery at the wharf-and the freight is paid by the British Government.
I did intend to-night to make a statement of considerable length to the House,' in more exact terms than the statement that I have made, regarding the activities of the Naval Service Department in relation to the war since the war broke out. As the hon. member for Pictou has seen fit to attack the Naval Service and to say that it has done nothing in connection with the war; as he has seen fit to complain because we had policemen instead of naval men to guard the dockyard at Halifax, in which respect we followed the example of the Imperial dockyards; at the risk of being somewhat tiresome, perhaps I had better make this statement to the House. Perhaps no better opportunity of doing so will present itself than is presented on the present occasion. I presume that my hon. friend in making this motion was actuated not so much by a desire to have the correspondence brought down as by a desire to have the opportunity of expressing his views with regard to the sins of commission of the Naval Service since the war broke out.

I did not assume that my hon. friend was going to make the statement to which he refers; I had thought that he would do that when in Committee of Supply. I did not make this motion for any other purpose than that which I stated in the few remarks that I made when I presented the motion to the House. My object was to see all the correspondence that can be brought down between this Government and the Imperial Government in regard to the reason why we are not sending men to the navy, as Newfoundland, South Africa and Australia are doing; also to ascertain the exact position of Canada on the sea today.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I accept at once the statement of the hon. member for Pictou, but perhaps this would be as good an occasion as any to give the House a very frank and somewhat comprehensive statement of what the Department of the Naval Service has done in relation to the war since it broke out. I may say that preparations having previously-

I should like to have
Your Honour's ruling upon the question of how a general statement of what the Naval Service has been doing has to do with the motion of the hon. member for Pictou, which is:
For a return showing a list of vessels, belonging to the Canadian Government which are on service under the provision of the Canadian Naval Act, and of all vessels not now in service and their present condition and suitability for service, and also for a copy of all letters, petitions or communications had by or With the Government in regard to the establishment of a Canadian naval brigade.
I am unable to see how the matters with which my hon. friend, purposes dealing are relevant to this motion. I think it would be' very much better if my hon. friend would not insist upon our exercising the courtesy which, perhaps, we should be glad to extend under ordinary circumstances, and make his statement when going into supply on the Naval Estimates, when the matter may be fully discussed. I am sure that if any private members were to proceed along the same line as that suggested by the hon. minister, you, Sir, would at once feel it your duty to call us to order; to rule that we were going too far afield in attempting to deal with the various matters that my hon. friend now purposes to deal with under this motion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member for Pictou went fully into the whole

scope of the Naval Service and its alleged deficiencies. I think the minister, under the circumstances, would be quite in order in making a statement as to what the Naval Service has done.
I said nothing about the commandeering of vessels, or about dockyards.

When we were discussing some matters the other day several members spoke, and, my hon. friend the Minister of Labour departed from the motion before the House. I followed him, and all at once my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, not improperly at all, suggested that we had better confine ourselves to the subject before the committee. The Chairman, although two or three members had been allowed-as no objection had been made-to discuss irrevelant matters, deemed it his duty to round us up, so to speak, and bring us back to where we belonged.

The hon. gentleman is entirely in error in the statement that he has just made. I called the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that he was dealing with Estimates of the Labour Department as if we were in committee, while as a matter of fact the Speaker was actually in the Ohair. I simply suggested that the House be put in order; that the Speaker leave the Chair, and that we go into Committee of Supply, so that the hon. gentleman could make the five, six, seven, or eight speeches that he attempted to make and did, make on that occasion. .It was only to put the House in order that I made the suggestion.

Perhaps I am wrong then in saying it was the Minister of Public Works, perhaps it was the chairman who did it. At all events I know I was brought to book, even although I was following alone the lines of the Minister of Labour; the chairman thought the discussion had gone far enough and he called me to order. I could not argue that the matter was relevant to the motion before the committee, and had to yield to the ruling of the chairman. I am sure that if any private member were_ to follow along the lines indicated by the Minister of Marine the Speaker would feel bound, very early in the discussion, to call him to order.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have no desire to violate or even to trespass on the rules of the 1061
House. But in this House I have always observed that on an application made for papers relative to any particular subject it has been open to any one speaking to the motion, to deal generally with the subject to which the papers related, and the statement I purposed making to-night as to the activities of the Naval Service would have been no more than an answer to the attack of the hon. member for Pietou (Mr. Macdonald) upon the Naval Department for its alleged lack of activity. I would submit that I am quite in order, although at the same time, if there is any doubt about it, I shall at once take my seat without dealing with that branch of the subject, as I have no desire to infringe upon the rules of the House. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, (Mr. Blain), as you are occupying the Chair only temporarily, it would be better not to put you to the necessity of ruling on a point of this sort on which there might be some difference of opinion. I have never seen such a point taken in the House before. As a rule there has been a wish on the part of the House to allow members to deal fully with any subject before it, as long as they confined their remarks to matters pertinent or relating to the particular subjects involved in the resolution. In this resolution the subject involved is undoubtedly the activities of the Naval Service, and so I think I am strictly in order; but as the point has been taken, and as I have already occupied a greater time than I intended to I shall not press the matter at this stage. My reason for speaking at such length was the unfounded attack of the hon. member for Pietou upon the work of the Naval Department since the breaking out of the war. I will only say, on behalf of the Naval Department, that I am prepared now or at any other time to fully justify what it has done, and to demonstrate to the people of this country that that department has faithfully discharged the onerous duties imposed upon it, and that what it has done has been in the public interest, and has been done, in most cases, with the full co-operation of and after consultation with the Admiralty; and that the Department is prepared to continue to the end of the war to do all it can under existing circumstances to bring the war to a successful termination and to assist in maintaining the supremacy of the British navy upon the high seas.

When I ventured tr
point out to the Minister of Marine that ] thought he was proposing to depart from

the resolution before the House,.
10 p.m. it was not, I can assure him, and I can assure you, with any idea of permanently preventing the minister from making the fullest statement he might desire to make to the House. But it occurred to me that .the proper time for such a statement would be when he comes to submit his Naval Estimates to the House, and then we would have a field day upon it. I would like to be able to talk for some little time upon that question, and I think it would not be very difficult to convince the people of this country, if we cannot convince the majority of the members of the House, that the Naval Department had absolutely fallen down so far as giving effective aid to the Empire or to Canada in connection with the war is concerned. In making his motion the hon. member for Pictou very properly called attention to the fact that when the war broke out the Niobe was out of commission. It is a fact which is known to the whole nation that at that time the tubes of the boilers had actually been filled with some sort of material to prevent them rusting, with the idea that the vessel would not be required at any time in the near future, and that all of this material had to be extracted after the war broke out, an operation which took weeks to accomplish. Thus, while, if the Niobe had been in commission, she might have performed most useful service in capturing valuable German prizes, she was absolutely of no value to the Empire. My hon. friend knows also that, in the year 1913, a report was brought down to this House having reference to the men who were on Board the Niobe, and making it public that they had been, by tacit consent, permitted to discharge themselves and to leave the vessel and go out of the service of His Majesty, and that no effort was made to retain them in the service. In the report of the Department of the Naval Service for the year ending 31st March, 1914, signed by the director of the Naval Service, Vice-Admiral Kingsmill, I find this extraordinary statement, which is not at all in harmony with the statement of the minister to-night:
The Government having decided not to continue His Majesty's ships Niobe and Rainbow in full commission, no recruiting was carried on during the year, and the programme of exercises and training laid down for these ships was not continued.
Is there there a suggestion that the Niobe was laid up because she had to go into dry dock or because she was not fit for service? There is no suggestion of that

kind by Vice-Admiral Kingsmill. Yet, in the face of that report, my hon. friend said to-night that this Government knew, and had known almost since they came into office, that danger was imminent.
In 1913, the naval discussion took place in this House, and. my right hon. friend the Prime Minister stated that in imagination he heard the distant booming of cannon, and the roaring of guns; that he almost felt that a great Empire war was at hand. Notwithstanding the fact that during the three years since he has pretended to this House-I do not use the word pretended in a harsh sense at all-that the Government had had foT a time reason to believe that danger was imminent, we find that in respect to those two ships, one upon the Atlantic, and the other upon the Pacific, the Director of the Naval Service says that the Government having decided not to continue them in special commission, no recruiting had been carried on during the year. The result was that when war broke out, the Niobe was unfit for service. Had she been fit for service, German vessels of great value might have been seized by her, and she might have done most effective work for Canada and the Empire. But she was not in condition to go to sea, and so it was with regard to the Rainbow. From this statement, she was not fully equipped, because recruiting had not been continued, and no effective efforts hud been made to keep her in full commission. Sir, had it not been for the presence in the Pacific Ocean of a Japanese cruiser which was prepared to guard the western coast of Canada, it is just possible that very serious damage might have been done to the cities upon the coast of British Columbia. Fortunately, it happened that the prediction of my right hen. friend, now the leader of the Opposition, made some years ago and when he was so strongly criticised because he attempted to icome to a friendly understanding with Japan, that the time might come when the ships of Britain and the ships of Japan vould be found side by side in the harbours of Victoria and Vancouver, was practically realized. It was, I believe, because a Japanese cruiser was there that v/e are in a position to-day to be thankful that the cities on the British Columbia coast were not attacked by German cruisers.
This report of Admiral Kingsmill proceeds-and you will see how it varies from the statement by the hon. minister tonight.

During the year, free discharge was given to those Canadians who entered the service as hoys and wished to avail themselves of the offer; In addition, many of the ranks and ratings lent from the Imperial Service have completed their engagement under the Canadian Government and returned to England, without being replaced, with the result that at present the ships are only manned by sufficient crew to keep them in good order and such state that, should they be required for sea service at any time, they could be placed in full commission without undue delay.
There is no suggestion there that the Niobe was not fit to be placed in commission; no suggestion that, if properly manned, she would not be able to do effective work. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has, most unfairly, I think, and in the most partisan spirit that I have seen displayed, during this session of Parliament, accused the Liberal party of deliberately preventing Canada from doing her part in the defence of the Empire by providing ships of war. He has charged, most unfairly, that not only did the Liberal party do what it could to present the Government's naval measure from passing in the House of Commons, but that the leader of the Liberal party exercised his influence in the Senate to prevent the passing of the Naval Bill which the Government by means of the closure had forced through the House of Commons. I say that that statement is absolutely urn founded. I do not believe that eitheT my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, or'any other member of the Liberal party ever exercised, or sought to exercise, the slightest influence upon any member of the Senate in respect to that Bill. I venture to say that my hon. friend the Minister of Naval Affairs has not a tittle of evidence upon which to found the extraordinary statement which he has mad,e tonight, and here, as a member of the Libera] party in this House, I challenge him to produce his authority for the statement he has made that the Liberal leader, or Liberal members of this House, went to the Senate and sought to induce the -members of that body to prevent the passage of the measure referred to. The statement, Sir, is unworthy of a gentleman occupying the high and, honourable position of minister of one of the most important departments of this Government. In the presence of the minister, who was not present when I made the statement a moment ago, I again challenge him to give to this House the authority upon which he made the extraordinary and unfounded statement that the Liberal leader, or any member of the Liberal party went to the Senate and used the slightest influence of any kind or description, directly or indirectly, upon members of the Senate in the action which they took upon that measure.
As my hon. friend has made a campaign speech to-night, in the most unfair way, and, as I have said, in the most partisan spirit, to influence the people of this country during this time of war and stress against the Liberal party by reason of its action with reference to the Naval Bill, let me remind him that what the Liberal party did was to propose and to support an amendment in this House which left the Government free to establish a naval unit, both upon the Atlantic and the Pacific, which would be available for the defence of Canada, and which would be at once placed at the service of the Empire in time of war. In 1913 the Bill, which this Government introduced, was defeated by the Senate, which simply adopted a resolution that before the country should make a contribution to the Imperial Government, contrary to what had been the understanding among public men on both sides in this country, the question should be submitted to the people. It would not have taken long. If hon. gentlemen upon the other side believed that the Empire was in danger, and that the granting of three dreadnoughts would be a means of saving the Empire, why did they not act upon the request of the Senate and submit the question to the people of this country? It would not have taken more than six weeks to decide the question; and yet they say that they thought it was of vast importance to the Empire that these dreadnoughts should be given. They did not dare to trust the question to the people of this country. There was something else that they did not dare to do. They did not dare to keep the promise which they had made to their Nationalist supporters in the province of Quebec. They had promised them that they would repeal the Naval Service Act. In the province of Quebec, from platform to platform, they went declaring that if the Conservative party were returned to power, almost the first step which would be taken would be the introduction of a measure to repeal the Naval Service Act. Sir, the Naval Service Act is upon the Statutes to-day, just as it left the hands of the Liberal party in 1910. As my hon. friend from Piotou (Mr. Macdonald) says: The department over which my hon. friend presides could not do anything to-day were it not for the Naval Ser-
Owing to the action of the Senate.

My hon. friend knows
very well what took place with regard to the building of war vessels.
