I was surprised to hear him say that our Government had kept the tenders^ for the building of the ten war vessels dangling before the people of this country, making people of different constituencies believe that the vessels were to be built at different places in Canada, in order to secure their favour and sup- -port.
That is what you told us yourself.
I did not.
It is a matter of public record .

My hon. friend is entirely wrong. He does not know the meaning of language when he says that. What I said was that the Naval Department called for tenders for the building of ten war vessels on the Atlantic coast. The only condition attached to the tenders was that the vessels were to be built so that there would be no violation of the compact which exists between Canada and the United States. Tenders were called, and the tenderers were allowed to select their own port for building. Some tenderers were in favour of Halifax, some in favour of Sydney, some in favour of Montreal, some in favour of Quebec, and one at least was in favour of building at the port of St. John. I am referring to Oammell, Laird & Company. What I said the other night-and I am surprised that the Minister of Public Works did not take a correct view of the statement which I made-was that these tenders were necessarily under consideration for quite a period. I told him that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries took the tenders to England and consulted the Admiralty with regard to the whole question, including the reliability of the various tenderers. Almost immediately after he came back, Parliament was dissolved. We did not deal with the question, of course, during the general election, but after the election the question came up as to what action should be taken. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who

had the tenders under consideration and had gone over the whole matter very carefully decided that the tender of Cammell, Laird & Company was the lowest. Their tender was to build the vessels at St. John, and my hon. friend knows it well. The records prove absolutely the truth of what I say. When my hon. friend came into office he found in his department the tenders of the various companies. He found that the deposits of all the tenderers, with the exception of Cammell, Laird & Company, had been returned; their deposit being still on hand as security for the performance of the contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: How does the hon. gentleman reconcile that with the statement made by his leader in Parliament; that if the Government of which my hon. friend was a member had continued in power, those vessels would have been under construction at the city of Montreal?
I beg my hon. friend's pardon, the right hon. leader of the Opposition never made that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's
pardon, he did.
I say he did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I say he did.
I say he did not, and I can say it with a far greater appearance of truth than my hon. friend can.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think those who know
my hon. friend will accept my statement as truthful quite as readily as his.
Order.

When my hon. friend so far forgets himself as to tell me or any hon. member of this House that he is not telling the truth, I think he ought to be asked to sit down until he gets in a calmer frame of mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am in as calm a frame of mind as my hon. friend. I asked him how it came that his -right hon. leader made that statement and he said that his hon. leader did not make it.
He did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I say he did. I have heard him make it, and it is on the record that he made it.

My hon. friend is entirely wrong. What the right hon. leader of the Opposition said was that if this Government had gone on with the Naval Service Act there would have been war
vessels built at the port, of Montreal. He was referring to this Government entirely. Let me say this, further, to my hon. friend: when the	minister	had decided that the	Cammell, Laird &
Company tender was the lowest, and that they were to build at the port of St. John, no leader of mine would have been sufficiently strong or have had sufficient influence to prevent my resenting such an injustice as passing over the lowest tenderer.
In that event, I would have had but one duty to perform, namely, to have gone back to my constituents and surrendered to them the trust which they had reposed in me, and said that I could no longer support a leader who could do such a rank injustice to any part of this country. Therefore, if I had been in my hon. friend's place, coming into office as Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the man who must initiate proposals to his colleagues, if I had submitted that proposal showing that Cammell, Laird & Company were the lowest tenderers proposing to establish a great shipyard and to build warships in my own constituency, if my leader then had said to me, as his leader must have said to my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries:	"Oh,
we cannot go on with the building of warships because we are pledged to the Nationalist party of Canada not to do it; Mr. Minister, you must return to Cammell, Laird & 'Company their .deposit What would have been my duty? It would have been to have left the Government, resigned my seat, and told the people of St. John that my constituency had been treated with rank injustice by my leader, and that I could no longer support him. Cammell, Laird & Company proposed to build at the port of St. John ten war vessels, four of them cruisers, three, I think, torpedo boat destroyers, and three of another class. My hon. friend knows that they were, because he has in his department all the papers, including the tender of Cammell, Laird & Company, from which he will see that every word I state is absolutely true. A considerable time before the war broke out, they would have-had, under the contract, at least two cruisers afloat prepared to do their part for the defence of Canada and of the Empire, because they were to have had two cruisers completed in three years and the whole contract completed in six years, Even although it would have been in the comparatively small city of St. John that the shipyard would have

been established, would it not have been a glorious thing for Canada that we would have had the vessels afloat; that we would have been in the same position as Australia is in to-day, that we would have been taking our part in the defence of our trade routes, protecting our transports and doing that work which Great Britain and Australia are to-ddy compelled to do for us? Would it not have been a glorious page that Canada would have written? And perhaps if we had had two of those cruisers afloat, they might have performed deeds just as magnificent as those which the Australian ship Sydney performed on the Pacific ocean.
What about the submarines?

The Government would also have been saved the necessity of buying those submarines, in regard- to which my hon. friend made to the British Government a statement which must disturb his conscience whenever he thinks of it, and which Mr. Plaza, the naval expert of the Chilean Government, said had not a tittle of foundation. My hon. friend will find on record that he sent a cablegram to the British Admiralty stating that the Chilean Government found themselves unable to take over those ships. I do not say that he deliberately misled the British Admiralty, but he was misled by that astonishing statesman who, for so many years, ruled the destinies of British Columbia, and who left that fair and rich province which, a few years ago, was supposed to have boundless resources, on the very brink of poverty and bankruptcy. It was that statesman who sent my hon. friend-that telegram which caused him to mislead the British authorities. Had he not been so misled, he would have been saved the necessity of going through that experience of buying for $1,150,000 two submarines which were to be built for the Chilean Government at a contract price of only $818,000, which were obsolete and incapable of passing the examination, and which the Chilean experts had rejected.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I thought those cruisers were for use on the Atlantic.
Mr: PUGSLEY: Those cruisers would have been available at whatever part of the coast of Canada it was thought desirable to place them; they would have belonged equally to all parts of Canada and they could have been sent wherever the Canadian Government or the British Admiralty thought well to send them. What position would Canada have been in were it not for what the 
Liberal party had done when it was in power? I called attention the other day to the entire failure of this Government to do anything to encourage the building of mercantile ships in Canada. They have seen, week after week, and month after month, since this war began, the shipping of Canada declining and the rates of transportation upon our- wheat, cattle, and lumber going up by leaps and bounds, until to-day they are a thousand, per cent greater than when the war broke out. My hon. friend knows what opportunities there are for building ships upon both the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts, and yet this Government are not taking a single step to encourage the building of ships. What have they done so far as war vessels are concerned? Were it not for the shiprepairing and shipbuilding, plants established at the port of Montreal by Vickers, Maxim & Company, under a contract which I made with that firm when I was Minister of Public Works, there would not be a single war vessel constructed in Canada since the war began. But dwing to what we did there, Vickers, (Maxim & Company have been able to repair war vessels as well as mercantile ships, and under a contract amounting to $10,000,000 given by the British Government to that much despised Fore River Shipbuilding Company, which my hon. friend three years ago said was in bankruptcy, that firm came ever, and, through Mr. Schwab, the millionaire, made an arrangement with Vickers-Maxim, under which a number of submarines were, within six months, constructed at the port of Montreal. I am proud that I, as Minister of Public Works in a Liberal Government, was the means of creating that magnificent establishment, which is an honour to the port of Montreal and a credit to the people of Canad.a, and which has been doing effective work for the Empire since the war began. We have a pretty good record in that respect, whereas the record of this Government could be shown upon one page, which, after you had written the whole record, would be absolutely blank. It is no pleasure to me to refer to these matters; but just before I take my seat I want to say that it is not a pleasing spectacle to have gentlemen on the other side, one after another, saying: "Oh, this is a time for party peace; this is a time when no one should criticise the Government, when no one should seek to create amongst the people of this country any want of confidence in this Government," and then to have my

hon. friend, one of the most influential members of the Government, make the most partisan speech which I have heard in this House for a number of sessions, raising the old issue of the naval question, charging us, as I have said, with improperly influencing the Senate and preventing that most extraordinary, and, shall I say, most iniquitous measure from becoming law. But let me tell the hon. gentleman that if he and his Government are determined to make these attacks upon us and upon our action in the past, which action we believe was influenced by patriotism and a sense of the duty we owe to this country and the Empire, we shall be prepared to meet them. He tells you, Mr. Speaker, that his Government could not have been wrong in 1913 because what they proposed to do had the full approval of the British Admiralty. And who was the spokesman for the British Admiralty at that time? Mr. Winston Churchill, the gentleman who is supposed to have brought disaster upon the British forces at the Dardanelles, the gentleman who, is held by many of the best-thinking people in England to be largely responsible for many of the disasters that have befallen the British Empire since this war began. He is the gentleman who actually thought that we could not build ships in this country because a firm foundation was required upon which to lay the keels-a statement that seemed to be approved by the Prime Minister, because he read Mr. Churchill's letter to the House, and apparently with approval. The right hon. gentleman (Sir Robert Borden) also read to this House, apparently with approval, the statement of Mr. Churchill that we could not build ships in this country because, forsooth, we required rivetters, and he did not know that [DOT] there were any rivetters to be got in Canada. Then too-ye gods ! think of it, Mr. Speaker -this gentleman, upon whose statement the Minister of the Naval Service relies, said that we could not build war vessels in Canada because cranes would be required lifting as much as a hundred and fifty tons. Why, even in the railway shops at Moncton you can find cranes that will lift the 90-ton locomotives as I would lift an envelope, and put it wherever it is required. Yet, the insuperable objection to building warships in Canada, according to Mr. Churchill, was that we had not heavy enough cranes. He is the gentleman who asked this Government to go back upon what Canada and Australia had agreed upon in 1909, and to reverse the naval
policy of the Empire. And this is the infallible statesman upon whose judgment they felt safe in' relying, and so placed the country in the humiliating position in which it stands to-day. I regret it, and I think all the best people in this country regret it also.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not purpose to follow the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) in his attack upon Mr. Churchill. That right hon. gentleman is eminently capable of speaking for himself, and his record qf accomplishment for the naval defence of the Empire will dwell in the memory of men, long after the futile and inconsiderable efforts of my hon., friend from St. John, shall have passed into deserved oblivion. I would like to correct him, however, in saying that the memorandum which was placed before this Parliament in the autumn of 1912 was from Mr. Churchill. It was not from Mr. Churchill but from the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, and the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty consist of the First Lord and at least four or five Sea Lords. They are technical men who are supposed to-know, and who I have no doubt do know, probably as well as my hon. friend, the needs of naval defence throughout the Empire, and the best course to be taken by any dominion of the Empire for giving the assistance which was then suggested. My hon. friend has endeavoured to pump up a little enthusiasm about the course he and his friends took in 1912 and 1913. He found it very difficult indeed to create any enthusiasm in his own mind, and still more difficult to create even the semblance of enthusiasm among the hon. gentlemen who sit behind him. But I think this may at least be said for the hon. gentleman that he is entitled, perhaps more than any other of them, to the glory, or whatever it may be, of preventing three Canadian dreadnoughts from flying the British flag to-day and assisting in the defence of the Empire. If he is still disposed to take pride in this-as apparently he does, for he said that the measure proposed by this Government for that purpose was one of the most iniquitous measures ever presented in this House, thus glorying in the defeat of ^ the attempt to enable Canada to participate in the naval defence of the Em-pbe he is entitled to all that glory if it is any satisfaction to him. It is a remark able spectacle for an hon. gentleman on that side to rise and ask why Canada was doing so little at th-e present -time in

the naval defence of the whole Empire. If the measure which my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) so deliberately and persistently obstructed, had passed the Senate, there would have been, a year ago, three ships, as powerful as any in the world, ready to assist the rest of the Empire's Navy in preserving the common rights and institutions and liberties of the whole .'Empire. That there is no such ship to-day is due to my hon. friend from St. John and to is friends, and to no one else. And -when he suggested there was an alternative proposition from the other side of the House in amendment to the Government measure, he conveniently forgets that the amendment proposed to postpone any action whatever until after a general election should be held in Canada.
I do not think I proposed that, nor that any one else proposed it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Does not the hon. member remember the terms of the amendment?	'
I do not think that was in it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He may not think so, but that does not alter the fact that it was in it. His memory is not so good on this as on some other points. I have a distinct recollection that the proposals offered by hon. gentlemen opposite involved the postponement of action until after the general election.
Has the right hon. gentleman the record there?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, but I will get it.
Did not the Prime Minister say that if his proposition was not accepted by the House, he would appeal to the country on it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I had said before, in the autumn of 1910, that I would do precisely what I did, that is, invoke the advice of the Admiralty and bring their advice to Parliament as a temporary measure. I went to the Admiralty and obtained their advice; that advice was given to the Parliament of Canada by the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty in these words:
The Prime Minister of the Dominion having inquired in what form any immediate aid that Canada might give would be most effective, we have no hesitation in answering, after a prolonged consideration of all the circumstances, that it is desirable that such aid should include

the provision of a certain number of the largest and strongest ships of war which science can build or money supply.
I brought that proposal to the House not as a permanent measure, but as a temporary measure. I told the House at that time that before the Government of Canada brought down a permanent measure for the co-operation of Canada in the naval defence of the Empire, we would submit a proposal to Parliament and to the people of Canada in order that they might know what the proposal was, and in order that they might exercise the right which they undoubtedly had of passing upon that proposal. That was a very clear, definite and * plain proposal; one which we endeavoured to .carry out so far as we were enabled to do so in the face of the opposition of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. Further than that, in 1914, immediately before the war broke out, we had made arrangements, in connection with the formulation of a permanent policy that Admiral Sir John Jellicoe, now commander in Chief of the British Fleet, should come to Canada for the purpose of consulting with us. Everything was arranged as to his visit here except the exact date, .but the breaking out of the war in August, 1914, prevented him from coming to Canada, as he had immediately to assume the responsible duties of Commander in Chief of the British Navy, which otherwise he would not have assumed until the following November or December.
Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House may very property desire to recede somewhat from the attitude which they took in 1912 and 1913. The hon. member for St. John showed a disposition to do that to-night. Hon. gentlemen were very merry in 1912, 1913, and 1914 at the idea that any danger confronted this Empire. If- any hon, gentlemen on this side of the House, having, regard to the conditions, which were pretty well understood in Europe, and fairly understood, perhaps, on this side of the Atlantic as well, ventured to address a word of warning to the people of this country as to the necessity of Canada's doing something to aid in the common defence of the Empire, his remarks were the subject of merriment and of jest on the part of hon. gentlemen on t'he other side of the House, and by no one more than by the hon. member for St. John, who vigorously applauded his leader when only six and a half months before the outbreak of the war the policy

and the view of the Liberal party were expressed by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition in these words:
X do not charge any Intention of deceit on the part of the Prime Minister in this regard, but I will charge deceit if, in the face of this evidence, we again hear of such a thing as an emergency.
That was six and a half months before the thunderbolt of war came upon this Dominion and this Empire. The right hon. gentleman continued in these words:
The German peril has disappeared, if, indeed, there ever was such a thing.
An absolute assurance to the people of [DOT]this country, given upon what evidence I do not know, that there was not the slightest danger of war between our Empire and Germany. Then he continued:
We know now how much the country and the Empire and the civilized world has been deceived upon that question of so-called emergency.
My hon. friends on the other side of the House are not prepared to cheer these words now as they did cheer them at the time that they were uttered. I well remember the thunderous applause which greeted every line that I have read when these words were uttered by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition. Then he continued as follows:
The Bill which was brought in last session, the Naval Aid Bill, was not even a, measure of emergency, although it was so-called. They introduced it upon the shallow pretence of emergency.
Tremendous cheers from hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House at that tiriie -but a depressing silence at present. Then the right hon. gentleman continued:
Emergency? Who speaks to-day of an emergency? Twelve months have passed since my right hon. friend the Prime Minister introduced his measure. Twelve months and more have passed since that time when he saw the German peril. He saw Germany almost ready to jump at the throat of Great Britain.
And when my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition reached that point in his remarks, his speech was interrupted by deafening applause which prevented him from continuing for some moments. Then, referring to myself, he continued as follows:
He saw clouds on the horizon, rent by lightning, and heard the murmurs and rumbling of cannon. But my right hon. friend to-day may live in peace. The climate is moderate and the sky is clear.
And within six and a half months after these words were uttered and that vain assurance had been given by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, this
Empire was involved in the present struggle. The right hon. gentleman continued his remarks in the same strain. On many other occasions during that session >the leader of the Liberal party and almost every hon. gentleman on the other side of the House used similar language. They jested at the idea that there was any danger, that there was any emergency, that there was any need. More than that, they said that the navy of Great Britain did not need any assistance. But the hon. member for Pictou this afternoon was greatly distressed because, as he asserts, the navy of the British Empire, although it has been increased beyond measure since the war broke out, is unable to discharge adequately the task of maintaining control of the seas and of protecting our commerce and our shores.
Let me give another illustration of the views of the hon. member for St. Johrp as expressed at that time by his leader. On March 15, 1913, hen the debate upon the Naval Aid Bill of 1912 had proceeded for several months in the face of -unparalleled obstruction, this was the language of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition:
When, some few months ago, in the earliest days of this session, members who support the Government were told that there was an emer-.gency in the affairs of Great Britain, and that Great Britain should receive the assistance of this country, they did not suspect, I am sure, that before the last vote would he taken they would have in their hands absolute evidence of the falsity of the assertion which was then made.
That is a fair statement of the attitude which hon. gentlemen took on the other side of the House. I observe that the hon. member for Rouville is in his seat. I wonder if I could find an extract from his Observations at that time. Perhaps they might be more productive of cheers and applause than those which I have read from the speeches of his leader. This is a very pregnant utterance of the hon. member for Rouville; I particularly invite attention to the closing sentence:
There seems to he at work, not only in England, hut in Great Britain, silent forces with the object of subduing, or reducing if possible, the greater freedom of the self-governing countries. Those silent forces have been at work very insidiously for the last fifteen or twenty years, never so actively as during the last five or ten years.	,
The present" policy of the Government is said to be the outcome of an emergency.
My hon. friend was endeavouring to bring up the ghost of autonomy, and this

was an attempt to prove that the building of three dreadnoughts by Canada to aid in the common defence of the Empire, the placing of those warships at the disposal of His Majesty the King for that purpose, subject to recall by the people of Canada whenever they chose to recall them, was in , some way a destruction or an impairment of our autonomy. The word autonomy was greatly in the mouths of the hon. gentleman opposite at that time-and I do not wonder that the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) smiles now at the folly of the words which he then uttered. He goes on to say:
That emergency was invented by those silent forces in order to obtain what they have been aiming at during the last twenty years.
You understand the suggestion. There was not any emergency, there was not any danger, there was not any peril. The assertion of danger and peril were due to the influence of those silent forces in Great Britain and in Canada which were aiming to destroy the autonomy of this Dominion. But the last sentence of all is really the gem of that particular utterance:
If you read the press to-day you can scent, so to speak, an alliance between Great Britain and Germany.
I	do not think that my hon. friend, with all the olfactory powers which he possesses, is able to scent very much of such an alliance to-day. Then, again, the hon. member for Rouville devoted himself to the question in one of the numerous debates which took place:
The so-called emergency has petered out.
Is it not a fact that at that time, or shortly before, Lord Haldane and Mr. Winston Churchill himself went to Berlin for the purpose of getting a closer alliance with Germany?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, it may be so, and in connection with that visit to Berlin it ought also to be remembered that the British Admiralty, consisting of the First Lord and of those technical and naval advisers with him who knew what the conditions were, had, asked us to
II	p.m. provide three of the most
powerful battleships in the world for assistance in the common defence of this Empire. My hon. friend said:
The so-called emergency has petered out I am afraid that the right honourable gentleman is under the influence of the scare-mongers of Great Britain

Well, after all, there is no danger.	-

My hon. friend was perfectly ready, without money and without price, to give this assurance to the people of Canada.
We have the panic-mongers of to-day trying to agitate the dominions; but the papers of yesterday give us the information that, far from fearing a war with Germany, His Majesty the King of Great Britain is sending the Prince of Wales to spend the Easter holidays at Berlin. The emergency and the panic are good for the children, but they will not appeal to the true Britisher or the stout hearted Canadian. All this is being engineered by some interests who control a certain press.
And we have had some information since the outbreak of war as to the message which Lord Haldane brought back from Berlin and as to the view which impressed itself upon the statesmen of Great Britain as. the outcome of- that visit. My hon. friend has no doubt seen, some utterances of the Prime Minister of Great Britain on this subject, made in Wales more than a year ago. I have not the slightest doubt that the message which came to us from the British Government, through the Admiralty, was to some extent influenced by the very fact that the British Government knew more than they thought it discreet or prudent to reveal to the public of Great. Britain, but which they did partially reveal to us, not only in the document laid on the table of the House, but in a certain other document which was communicated to some other hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House and which said far more than the document which has been made public in this country. And it was with that knowledge that certain hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House took their stand upon this question with a view of preventing the people of Canada, the Parliament of Canada, the majority of the Commons of Canada, from carrying out a proposal which as I believed then, and believe now, was undoubtedly in the best interests of this Empire, and which constituted a duty that the people of Canada at that time owed to the whole Empire for the purpose of its common defence. Then my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) on the 9th day of June, 1914, a little more than a year before the war broke out, said this:
Bast year he (Sir Robert Borden) brought forward his contribution policy to meet an emergency which did not exist, and which has burst like a bubble. That policy made Canada the laughing stock of Great Britain and of all the other Overseas Dominions.
Who thinks of his emergency to-day? I dare say that not one of his blatant jingoes of the city of Toronto believes in that emergency today. It was a scare-line policy to recoup the

jingo capitalists of Winnipeg, Toronto, and Montreal, who had financed the Tory party in 1911 against the farmers, the taxpayers of Canada.
No more mention is made of the $35,000,000 ; the Admiralty does not want our gold any more, the trick has heen played out.
These are samples of the manner in which hon. gentlemen opposite met a proposal which was made in absolute good faith by the present administration to the Parliament of Canada. We went to Great Britain asking fairly, definitely, carefully, for the best opinion of the experts of the Admiralty and of the British Government as to the course which Canada ought to take, having regard to the possible necessity of some immediate steps being necessary for the common defence of this Empire. We came back with that document exactly as they had handed it to us and placed it before Parliament, and based our measure on it. I could give a great many more extracts illustrating the position that hon. gentlemen opposite took with regard to it. Those I have given are, I think, enough. I venture to 'say that *in these circumstances it does hot lie in the mouths of hon. gentlemen opposite to reproach this Government at least with the fact that we have not been able upon the ocean to play the part that Canada, in common with Australia iand New Zealand, ought to have played in this great war. When war broke out, or very shortly after, in 1914, I communicated.with the British Government as to what they desired us to do in this respect. Sir John Jellicoe was not able to come to Canada by reason of the fact that it was necessary for him to assume at once the command of that great fleet which has kept its vigil in the North sea, and which has maintained so close a guard that, with very infrequent exceptions, the whole German navy has been shut up in the Baltic or in the Kiel- canal. As I say, Sir John Jellicoe was not able to come, but I did communicate with the British Government. I asked them this question:	We are proposing to give you
every assistance in our power for the purpose of bringing this war to an honourable and triumphant conclusion; is it your desire that we should endeavour to assist in naval affairs, or do you desire that we should confine our efforts to raising forces in order that we might assist you in that way. The answer which I received from the British Government was this: They preferred that the effort- of iCanada should be devoted to the raising of military forces, to dispatching them across the ocean, to sending them with the other forces of the Empire to meet
the enemy at the front. And for that reason, since the opening of the war, we have not embarked upon any proposal to acquire ships, or to do anything in a great way in the naval line. We have devoted our energies and our efforts to raising military forces according to the expressed desire of the British Government.
So, we have a very clear conscience as to our efforts in this war; a very clear conscience as to the effort which we made in 1912-13 to assist in the naval defence of the Empire by the provision of the three ships. That effort, unfortunately, was not successful, for the reasons which I have mentioned. But in the line along which our efforts in this war have been directed, 1 venture to think that, during the past 18 or 19 months, we have accomplished very much more than any one of us would have believed possible on the 4th day of August, 1914. We sent, in the first instance, within six weeks after the outbreak of the war, 30,000 men, and, within about two months ot the time when hostilities broke out, they were across the Atlantic. Since that time, the total enlistments in Caflada have run up to 275,000 men, and the troops have gone forward, fully armed and equipped and in most cases, organized in every branch of the service. More than that, when they have gone to the front, they have shown themselves worthy, both of the great cause for which they are fighting, and of this Dominion which sent them forth to do battle, not only for the liberties of Canada and of the Empire but for the liberties of the whole world.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (-South Cape Breton):
speechtext:
It is perhaps rather unfortunate that at this stage of the session, this particular question should have aroused such partisanship in this Assembly. I am not going to say who may, or who may not have been in fault in promoting this partisanship. My hon. friend from Pictou has moved a resolution asking:
For a return showing a list of vessels, belonging to the Canadian Government which are on service under the provision of the Canadian Naval Act, and of all vessels not now in service and their present condition and suitability for service, and also for a copy of all letters, petitions or communications had by or with the Government in regard to the establishment of a Canadian naval brigade.
The most of us know fairly well what that list of vessels is, and the most of us also know that that list of vessels is too small for Canada at the present time. The

right hon. leader of the Government has made a very serious charge against the hon. member for St. John. He has charged that hon. member with having obstructed the promotion by the Government of its naval policy. He said further that had it not been for the hon. member for St. John, this country would, at the present time, be represented in the British Navy by three dreadnoughts, which would be of great assistance to the Motherland.
May I make a charge against the Government? May I charge the Government with being remiss in their duty in not having this country defended at the present time by seven fast cruisers, with the usual auxiliaries to cruisers? May I charge this Government with negligence . in this matter, because if they had followed the programme laid down in the Naval Act, and by the Liberal Government in 1911, we would have had our coasts guarded at this present moment by seven fast cruisers and the necessary auxiliaries? My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has spoken of emergencies, and from the hand-book which he held in his hand, and which, I have no doubt, was intended for the use of Conservative speakers during the campaign which it was thought would probably take place some time ago, he quoted from speeches of hon. members on this side of the House to the effect that there was no emergency. What did all this talk of emergency mean? Where did the emergency exist? In the naval debate in this House, and I watched it very carefully, the emergency was supposed to be in the North sea, and this Government proposed to meet that emergency by giving three dreadnoughts to the British navy. Has there been an emergency in the North sea since this war commenced? Is there an emergency in the North sea to-day? Are the dreadnoughts and cruisers of Great Britain not quite capable of handling any emergency that exists in the North sea to-day? At the present time, the battle ships of Germany are imprisoned in the Kiel canal, thanks to the efficiency and capability of the British Navy in the North sea. If there is an emergency at the present time in regard to the navy of the Empire, that emergency exists off the coasts of Canada;,; because it is a notorious fact that, since the war commenced, the coasts of Canada have not been defended.
My hon. friend spoke of the British Admiralty having prepared a memorandum

which had been brought down in this House. But that was not the first memorandum from the British Admiralty that had been brought down with regard to the Empire's defence on the seas, and to the defence, that would be contributed to the Empire by the overseas dominions. In 1910 or 1911, there was a conference in Great Britain, and a memorandum was drawn up. My hon. friend from Pictou-in the session of 1911, asked this question:
Has there been any change made in the terms of the memorandum of the Conference between the British Admiralty and the representatives of Canada and Australia as set out on page 461 of the Minutes of the preceding Imperial Conference of 1911?
And the answer is, " No." That -answer was given in this House on November 29,	1911. What was that conference?
I am not going into that question, but I want to say that the naval policy of the late Liberal Administration was recommended by the British Admiralty. For proof of that, I have to go no further than the words of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. In the session of 1911 I put certain questions on the Order Paper with regard to the Naval Service Act. Question 3 was: "Were the plans for these proposed vessels submitted to and approved by the British Admiralty?" And the answer was; " The plans were prepared by the British Admiralty." And, that was the policy of the Liberal Administration in this country. If there is an emergency in the British Navy to-day, the emergency is for young men to-take the place of those who have been in *the service for years, whose heads are hoary and bodies weak from length of service. The British Admiralty are calling for recruits to fill up vacancies in the British Navy. What is the Minister of Marine doing to fill that need? What did the Naval policy of this Government in 1912 do towards meeting that emergency? We are not giving men to Great Britain for the Navy, not a single one. The urgent need of Great Britain to-day is not ships in the North Sea, but men for her navy, and fast cruisers . to protect the coasts of Canada. This perhaps is not a very fitting time to enter upon a discussion which in years past has been of the most partisan character ever seen in this House, but the subject is up and it is just as well for us to have a heart-to-heart talk about it. If the Liberal policy had been carried out-and there was no change in it, there is no change in it to-day, except that the present Government refuses to build ships under the Naval Service Act-

it would not have been necessary lor this Government to buy two submarines which were refused by the Chilean Government, to protect the shores of British Columbia. This Government would not have been in the humiliating position of having to depend upon the cruisers of Japan for the protection of- our Pacific coast, or of harving to accept the services of private individuals in this country to fit out the only cruisers we have in this country which are capable of escorting Canadian troops overseas to fight the battles of the Empire. Canada's great need to-day is cruisers to convoy our troops across to England, and if the Liberal policy had been carried out by the present Government as it should have been carried out, at the present time we should have cruisers on both our Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and we should be able to escort our troops across ourselves. Nor should we have to depend upon the cruisers of Japan for the protection of our Pacific coast. But, apart altogether from these two different naval policies, I charge that' this Government has not done its duty since the war began. I charge it with not having undertaken to get from the ship-building firm in Montreal submarines which would have guarded our coast, instead of buying submarines which, in the opinion of men in this and other countries who are in a position to know, are no good. At the present time there is. in the city of Montreal a ship-building firm which is turning out submarines good enough {or Great Britain to buy. Does the Minister of Marine think that he is doing his duty as a responsible minister Of the Crown in this crisis, by sitting idly by and not getting that shipbuilding concern in the city of Montreal to build submarines for the defence of our coast? This firm is perfectly capable of building first-class submarines. The submarines they turn out are so good that they can travel from Canada to the Motherland under their own power.
The assistance which this Government proposed to give under their naval policy is not the assistance which the Mother Country requires to-day. We need no more dreadnoughts in the North Sea or on the coasts of France and England; but we do need fast cruisers on the coasts of Canada, to do for this country what the Sydney and the Melbourne are doing for Australia. It must have been a matter of pride to the Australians when, after a search of weeks and weeks by the cruisers of the British Admiralty, the Sydney-the fulfilment of the policy outlined and approved by the British
Admiralty in 1910; located and destroyed the Emden, the greatest scourge to British commerce in this war. Do not my hon. friends on the Government benches believe, in all seriousness, that it would have been better for Canada and the Empire if they had carried out the policy that was agreed upon at the Imperial. Conference in 1910? We should then be in the position *of Australia; our coasts would have some protection, which they have not at the present time.
I am not aware that this Government has asked our Canadian boys' to enlist in the British Naval Service. My hon. friend from Pictou put a question on the Order Paper some time ago asking what has been done in that regard, but I have not noticed that any answer has been given up to the present time. If this Government does not ask for recruits to fill up vacancies in the British Navy, I say they are not doing their duty in the present crisis. New Zealand has done it; Australia is doing it with regard to her own navy, and South Africa has- sent from 8^000 to 10,000 naval Teservists to the British Navy. But Canada has done nothing. It is true that Canada is doing a great deal in the way of raising military units, and that Canadians are doing well as regards recruiting. But I venture to assert that there are along the coast of the Pacific, and along the shores of the Maritime Provinces, thousands of people who do not care to enlist in the Canadian Expeditionary Forces, but who would jump at a chance of getting into the British Navy, and serving the Empire in that way. The British Navy needs them, and I say that the Minister of Marine and this Government will not be doing their duty until they help supply this need. I do not say that they do not want to do it. I do not say that they are disloyal, or that they the unaware of the fact that these men are needed; but to one who has followed the political history of this country for the last four or five years, it does seem passing strange that nothing has been done in that regard. Is it to fulfil an engagement that the Government, previous to 1914, had with the Nationalist party of this country that there would be no recruits from the province of Quebec or elsewhere to fill vacancies either in the Canadian navy or in the navy of Great Britain? I am not going to make the charge, but people, who have studied this question and who have watched events in connection with our naval policy, may well be suspicious that such is the case.
My Ron. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) said the other day that the

Niobe and the Rainbow were dismantled because they were of no use. But, I think we have it from the lips of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, in an answer which he made last session to a question, that the Niobe was doing splendid work guarding the coast of Nova Scotia; that she was in splendid condition, thanks to himself and his department; and that she was one of the best cruisers on the Atlantic coast. ' It must strike Canadians, and certainly Nova Scotians, as passing strange to see this same Niobe, which the minister said last year was doing splendid work in patrolling our coasts, tied up to-day at a wharf in Halifax with some kind of a house built on her deck with sleeping rooms for landlubbers. If the Niobe was a good ship and performed splendid work a year ago, why is she thus relegated to the scrap heap at the present time? I did not have the pleasure this evening of listening to -the speech delivered by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and I do not know whether he has given any explanation; but if he has not done so, the people of Sydney, Halifax and of every other port in the province of Nova Scotia are demanding an explanation and will bring him to an accounting for having thus relegated the Niobe to the scrap heap in Halifax harbour. , There is one thing which my hon. friend the minister has excelled in. While he has allowed the nucleus of the Canadian navy to go to the dogs, he has not neglected those people along the shores who had motor boats fifteen or twenty feet long; he has sent those boats down to the coast of Newfoundland for what purpose I do not know, unless for the purpose of drawing salaries for the crews' and day's wages for the boats, because they could not be of any benefit in the world for defence_or offence, unless it be offensive to see them run around our shores, with their crews coming occasionally into the harbours and having a good time. It is current gossip-I do not know how true it is-that the owners of these motor boats are each receiving $75 a day. The people of Nova Scotia are looking at this matter with ridicule. What earthly good could a motor boat be in Newfoundland, of all places? If the minister had allowed those boats to run in and out of Sydney or Halifax or some of the other harbours, it would not have been so bad. Those 'boats were not able to cross to Newfoundland under their own steam, but were taken across on the little ship Margaret. Yet, the minister has those vessels on his
list for the defence of Canada! Mr. Speaker, you should have seen them and you would certainly rest secure in your home down in Cumberland county to know that there were being carried back and forth between the city of Sydney and St. John last summer on board the little cruiser Margaret, two motor boats, one about fifteen feet keel and the other about eighteen feet keel. What they did after they reached Newfoundland I know not, but it must have 'been a source of great relief to yourself and to other loyal Nova Scotians to know, that for at least two months those two boats were carried hack and forth on three occasions on the deck of a snug little cruiser called the Margaret. It must have been a great relidf to the British Government to know that this Government had made such wonderful strides in the defence of -our Canadian coasts and I have no doubt that the names of these boats, with the names of other valuable assets, which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries made to his naval brigade last summer, will appear on the list if this motion passes for the production of the names of those vessels.
The question as to who was right and who was wrong in 1911, whether or not the Government knew that there was going to be a war, and whether the Opposition did not know, there was going to be a war, is one that perhaps will never be decided during the lifetime of the present generation or, of the next,' but the fact is that we have in this country to-day to meet conditions which confront us. The fact is that our Canadian shores are undefended, and while the Premier has charged the Opposition with	being
responsible for the absence of three dreadnoughts from the Imperial navy, I want to charge this Government with having our coasts on the Pacific and on the Atlantic undefended, owing to the fact that they did not carry out even partially the policy of the late Administration. If the Government saw war clouds; if they knew that war was coming, they were making very little preparation for it. The Niobe, to which the minister a year ago gave a good character as being one of the best cruisers on the coast was then, as she is now, tied up to a wharf in the port of Halifax, and I understand that the Rainbow is in the same positiorr-on the Pacific. If they saw the war clouds; if they knew the war was coming, and that' there were German cruisers along our coasts, they were remiss in their duty if they did
r.Mr. Carroll.]

not at that time-without waiting until the war was on, t-o buy two submarines that were worthless-provide a shipbuilding firm to build and equip submarines which could be of use in defending both the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts of this country. '
Mr. OLIVER J. WILCOX (North Essex): My hon. friend from South Cape Breton during the course of his remarks stated that he did not hear the speech of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I feel sure that had he had the privilege of listening to that speech, he would never have been guilty of making the speech he did because the minister answered every allegation put forward by my hon. friend. It is to be regretted that at this time in the history of our country when we are involved in a gigantic struggle, this Government and its supporters, who are burdened with responsibility-
What is worrying my hon. friend?

-such as no Government has been burdened with since Confederation, or probably ever will be again after this war is over, should have, day after day and night after night, to defend most vicious partisan attacks, that are entirely uncalled for.
I do not propose-though I suppose I could make as great a noise as some of our hon. friends opposite-to enter into a lengthy debate on this question, but I do want to answer a point or two that have been raised in this discussion. My hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) and my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald; raised the old bogey of the Nationalists again. They do love to try to associate this Government with the Nationalists. Well, whatever else may be said, one thing about the Nationalists is absolutely sure, and that is that in the naval measure the Nationalists allied themselves with the members of the Opposition, The Government side committed themselves to a policy of strengthening the naval defence of the Empire, and the Liberal party said that should not be done, and that was the position that the Nationalists took also. So, on this question, they sleep in the same bed.
My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) stated that the right hon. leader of the Opposition had never said that the Canadian navy, as proposed by the late Government, would be built in Montreal Here are the words of the right hon. gentleman as 107

reported in Hansard of 1913, volume 1, page 1034:
Yes, we thought as the general elections were coming, that it would not he fair, in a matter of this kind, which was at issue between the two parties, to award the contract, in case there might be, as there was, a change of government. X say now that the Government in power would have been better advised if they had awarded the contracts, and, had they done so, we would at the present time have under, construction on the stocks in Montreal, four cruisers and six destroyers.
Here is a very distinct statement by the leader of the Opposition that the total number of ships embodied in his Bill would be constructed at Montreal; and this, notwithstanding the fact-and I am surprised to think that the Liberals would do this- that in practically every constituency where there was water the prospect was held out to the electors that these boats would be built in that constituency. So far was this carried that in a meeting in Collingwood the opponent of the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) alleged to the electors that these boats would be built in Collingwood. When the hon. member spoke after his opponent, and told the electors that the Welland canal was not large enough to let the boats out of Lake Erie, his opponent was on the horns of a dilemma It all goes to prove that the thing was a political scheme from beginning to end.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to say they were not going to build even one in St. John?

Not one, they were all to be built in Montreal. But during the election they were to be built where the most votes were to be had. So the statement of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was absolutely right, and the hon. member for *St. John was wrong, as he generally is. Now, it is getting late, and I move the adjournment of the debate.
Mr. MACDONALD': I desire to say a word or two before the motion is carried.
Does the hon, gentleman want to go on?
Yes, I would like to say a few words.
I withdraw my motion.
When I presented this motion it was with the idea that this country was entitled to do something to assist the navy of the Empire in this war,

and I felt that in so far as the results of the Naval Service Department's efforts in this matter on the Atlantic seaboard were concerned, they were entirely inadequate. My hon. friend the Minister of the Naval Service (Mr. Hazen) proceeded to raise the old, question of the naval policy which was so thoroughly threshed out three years ago. He even ventured to make the statement, which is made by the unthinking in this country, that if Canada was not doing anything for the navy 1 in this war the fault lay with the Liberals. He entirely overlooked the point raised by my resolution. The speech of the right hon. the Prime Minister was enough to surprise any old member of this- House who can remember the speeches of the right hon. gentleman in 1909, when he declared that it was time for Canada to begin the construction of a Canadian navy. He went up and down that province justifying that position, and telling the people of Nova Scotia that this was the hour of destiny for them, that because of the adoption of a policy of speedy construction of a Canadian navy there was to come to them once more the maritime supremacy which they formerly enjoyed. That was the declared policy of the Opposition of that time, when the gentlemen representing the Liberal Government went to Great Britain in pursuance- of the resolution which the right hon. gentleman had supported. Those representative's made the arrangement with the Admiralty, and that arrangement was made by Australia at the same time. The Australians went back to enter upon the carrying out of the policy which was agreed upon, just as Sir Wilfrid Laurier came back to Canada to enter upon the policy agreed upon with him.
When I hear these flambuoyant speeches from the Minister of Naval Service and the right hon. Prime Minister, I wonder if they spoke to the Right Hon. Mr. Hughes, Premier of Australia, who went through this country a month ago, and whom they made a member of their Privy Council, in regard tQ the question as to whether or not a policy of contribution, so far as naval matters are concerned, is the correct one. I am afraid that if hon. gentlemen admit the Right Hon. Mr. Hughes to their conferences on the naval question very often, there will be a very marked division of opinion amongst them, because the Right Hon. Mr. Hughes glories in the fact that he was the father of the Australian navy idea. If these gentlemen who thought that Australia was

no good, that she could not send any men, that she could not build any ships, had asked the Right Hon. Mr. Hughes as to what is the proper policy for Canada and as to what was the proper policy in 1911, he would have expressed an opinion which would cause hon. gentlemen to realise that the speeches of the Minister of Naval Affairs and of the Prime Minister this evening were entirely beside the mark; he would have said that he, at least, did not believe in the policy of contribution. The Prime Minister of this country does not believe in a policy of contribution. He will not stand up in this House and say that when he pronounces what he always calls his permanent policy, that policy is1 bound to be a policy of the construction of Canadian ships, built right here in Canada and manned by Canadians. In the absence of the Prime Minister, I say to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries- that I defy the right hon. gentleman, since this question has been raised by him and his minister to-night, to stand up when the Naval Estimates are under discussion, and say that he is opposed, as the permanent policy in Canada in the matter of naval affairs, to the policy which Australia and every other overseas dominion has adopted. If he will not do so, what is the use of hon. gentlemen trying to wave the flag? What is the use of their beating tom-toms and going round the country talking about what they would have done; In 1910 the right hon. gentleman who leads this House 'discovered' that some political fruits might be gathered through the assistance of the hon. member for St. Antoine and one or two other gentlemen who could, by money and other methods, make a deal with Mr. Bourassa, the Nationalist, in the province of Quebec, to continue the propaganda against Sir Wilfrid Laurier. That lion, gentleman, so far as the policy of construction is concerned, has laid low. He never attacked it, never denied it at any time during all his career; nor has he ventured to do so to-night. There are sitting behind him in this House to-day twenty-six men who are opposed to all kinds of naval assistance to Great Britain. The right hon. gentleman in 1911 took into his Cabinet three men who were pledged to this same thing. He has been juggling with that Nationalist combination ever since, trying to placate them, trying to keep the tail from wagging the dog. The right hon. gentleman says we should play the part that Australia played, while he

knows in his heart as well as anybody does that the reason why we did not play the part that Australia played may be attributed solely to. him. He is the man who prevented us from playing the part that Australia played. When history is written on this questionwhen men look at these things with clearness and certainty, entirely apart from political prejudice, the attitude of the right hon. gentleman will be made clear. Why, he was in the hole after 1911 in respect of this Nationalist combination, to whom it is said he pledged himself against doing anything in the way of a 'Canadian navy-which was the objectionable thing in their minds- although he had voted for it in 1909; and he had to get up something to take its place. From the remarks of hon. gentlemen opposite, one would almost think that the right lion, gentleman, with the vision of a seer, had known that this war was going to come about- that there was to be an assassination in Serbia, and that events -were to follow in the Balkan countries 'by which the war should 'be commenced.
They knew it all.

Of course; they had heaven-born inspiration which gave them knowledge of all these things. Yet some months after the war began there was a good deal of talking about whether Great Britain was right in taking part in this war; reams of documents were written and printed to satisfy British people the world over that Britain was right in entering upon this war. All that was done to convince the public mind as to what we should do in regard to this matter. Speaking in the City Temple in London on November 10, 1914, Mr. Lloyd George made this declaration at a time when there was matter of argument in Great Britain with reference to the war:
When this war broke out, we were on better terms with Germany than we had been for fifteen years. There was not a man in tire Cabinet who thought that war with Germany was a possibility under present conditions.
Lloyd George, of course, knew what he was talking about, If the British cabinet did not think that war with Germany was a possibility, then the hon. Minister of Naval Service and the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada, if they knew about all these things, knew more than the people in Great Britain. If that be the case, they must have had a wonderful second-sight. Yet they say to the people: we knew this war was coming; hence it was that our policy of 107i
contribution to please the Nationalists, based on an alleged emergency, was the right policy. I was absolutely, surprised at the right hon. Prime Minister to-night when, the question having been raised by the hon, member for St. Johns as to what the Liberal policy was in 1913, he said: we had included in our resolution the condition that anything that was to be done was to be subject to the approval of the people of Canada. I am going to put on Hansard the amendment submitted at that time by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, so that there will be no question about the matter. It is to be found on page 1038 of Hansard of 1918, and is as follows:
That all the words after the word 'That' be struck out, and the following be substituted therefor:

'This House declines to concur in the said resolution and orders that the same be referred back to the committee with instructions to amend the same in the following particulars, namely, to strike out all the words after clause (a) and substitute therefor the following:
The memorandum prepared by the Board of Admiralty on the general naval situation of the Empire and communicated to this House by the right hon. the Prime Minister on December 5th shows that several of the most important of the foreign powers have adopted a definite policy of rapidly increasing their naval strength.
That this condition has compelled the United Kingdom to concentrate its naval forces in home waters involving the withdrawal of ships from the outlying portions of the Empire.
That such withdrawal renders it necessary that Canada without further delay should enter actively upon a permanent policy of naval defence. -
That any measure of Canadian aid to Imperial naval defence which does not employ a permanent policy of participation by ships owned, manned and maintained by Canada and contemplating construction as soon as possible in Canada, is not an adequate or satisfactory expression of the aspirations of the Canadian people in regard to naval defence and is not an assumption by Canada of her fair share in the maintenance of the naval strength of the Empire.
This House regrets to learn the intention of the Government to indefinitely postpone the carrying out by Canada of. a permanent naval policy.
It is the opinion of this House that measures should be taken at the present session to give effect actively and speedily to the permanent naval policy embodied in the Naval Service Act of 1910 passed pursuant to the resolution unanimously approved by this House in March 1909.
This House is further of the opinion that to increase the power and mobility of the Imperial navy by the addition by Canada under the above Act of two fleet units, to be stationed on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of Canada, respectively, rather than by a contribution of money or ships, is the policy best calculated to afford relief to the United Kingdom in respect to the burden of Imperial naval defence, and in the words of the Admiralty memorandum to re-

store greater freedom to the movements of the British squadrons in every sea and directly promote the security of the dominions ; and that the Governement of Canada should take such steps as shall lead to the accomplishment of this purpose as speedily as possible.'
That was the policy of the Liberal party in 1913. That is the resolution which we debated in this Parliament during the long session. And to-day, if that resolution had been adopted and if this Government had been true to the statements made by their own leader and by the Minister of Trade and Commerce,- whose impassioned utterance in 1909 as to Canada's duty to enter actively upon the line of naval assistance will always be remembered by those of us who were here, had they been true to themselves and followed that policy of ours, which was the Australian policy, we would not need to have the Sydney and the Australia defending our Atlantic coast to day; we would have had ships of our own doing it. But what had these hon. gentlemen to do? All they had to do was to go on under the provisions of the Canadian Naval Act placed on the Statute book in 1910. All they had to do was to ask Parliament to vote $35,000,000 to be expended under its provisions and not by way of contribution. But my hon. friends were afraid of the Nationalists and did not venture to do that. Had they, in 1913, asked Parliament for a sum of money to be spent under the provisions of the Canadian Naval Service Act of 1910, the money would have been voted. They knew that but they did not do it. What did they do?
They did nothing in 1913.
12	midnight. Now, in 1916, we learn for the first time that the Premier of this country, asked Sir John Jellicoe, in 1914, to come out to Canada. Mark you, this gentleman who knew all about the war coming on, who was certain about it, was proceeding, with such leisurely haste in regard to the matter that, doing nothing at all of any kind in 1913, not buying or building submarines, not buying or building vessels in any way, he leisurely suggested to Sir John Jellicoe, on the eve of this war, which he knew was coming on, to come out to Canada and talk over the question of what? Of an emergency assistance? Not at all, but of the permanent naval policy of Canada which he was going to enter on in 1914 i If non/ gentlemen, in view of these facts, which cannot be denied and which are simply a repetition of history, expect to be able to presume on the credulity of the people of this country, 
to such an extent that they will believe that the Premier had any information in 1914 that this war was coming on when he
was leisurely going to talk over the situation with Sir John Jellicoe as to the permanent naval policy, they overestimate the credulity of the Canadian people.
My hon. friend says that if their resolution had been passed there would have been three dreadnoughts in the North Sea. Would there? We would have had to go to England and borrow the $35,000,000 and hand the money over to the British Government and say to them; Please, Mr. Government, we , are entirely an inadequate people in every way, we are not to be compared with the overseas Dominion of Australia which has gone ahead and done its own financing and its own business, but please, lend us $35,000,000, Mr. Britisher, and then take it and build our ships for us ! That was the proposition, when they could have voted the money and built the ships themselves for the common defence. But they were playing to the Nationalists on that proposition. If they had laid down the keels of the vessels in 1913, under the provisions of the Naval Service Act, we would have had vessels that would have been of some use as coast defence vessels in this country to-day, and we would have had something of real value in the present situation. One does not need to follow in this House the story of this naval question in order to arrive at a clear view of the situation. When I hear the Prime Minister of this country stand up in this Parliament and declare that the position he took in 1909 vras incorrect when he stated that what we should do was to stand for a speedy construction of a Canadian navy, when I hear him doing that frankly as a public man, then I will believe he has changed his opinion. But he has never done it up until to-day. He has talked about contributions and about emergencies and all that, but he has never expressed this change of opinion, because he is expecting some day, when he has a permanent policy, to adopt the policy of the Liberal party to this matter.
This expression was entirely beside the proposition which I submitted to the House. My right hon. friend, through juggling with words, attempted to make the House believe on the question of whether we should recruit men in Canada for a naval reserve, that Great Britain did not want men to be recruited in Canada for the navy. If that was his idea he was trying to lead this House along lines which were incorrect. What did he do? He took 250 men from the

Royal Navy Reserve out in British Columbia and he put them on these vessels on the Atlantic. They were on the Niobe two months ago. To-day he is calling for recruits out in Vancouver in order to fill up that reserve. Why is he calling them if they are not wanted? What is the meaning of this statement, for instance, that was made by Dr. Macnamara on the floor of the British House of Commons? Dr. Macnamara was asked by Mr. Bellaire, the well known naval writer, who was in the British House of Commons, as to what South Africa was doingj and he said:
Tthe offer of the services of a number of the South Africa Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve was gladly accepted by the Admiralty, and the men are now attached to the Royal Naval Division in this country. It was understood that they wished to serve as a unit representing their corps.
Did the Prime Minister ever make to Great Britain the offer which was made by Cape Colony in that respect? What does it mean that Australia has sent so many men to serve in the British Navy? What did it mean when Newfoundland, the colony adjacent to my province, sent 1,600 men to serve in the navy? These men are not reservists, as my hon. friend says. Some of them were reservists, but numbers of them came from the outports, who were simply sailors, fresh from the sea, who went over and enlisted in the navy in preference to enlisting in the army. And why did they want to go into the navy? Simply because the sea appealed to them. The navy proposals in regard to pay and allowances were not as attractive as those of the army. My hon. friend will tell me that Cape Colony made an offer of men which was accepted. Australia made an offer of men which was accepted, and so did Newfoundland. Does my hon. friend the minister mean to say that if we had offered the same kind of men for the vessels of the British Navy that our offer would have been refused? I will wait to see the papers which my hon. friend has promised to bring down before I believe anything of the kind.
We have heard a great deal about the Niobe. I want to say just a word or two in regard to that vessel before I conclude. In the first place, let me say that the Niobe is a first class cruiser of 11,000 tons. She was built in 1909, and her armament consisted of 16 6-inch guns, 12 12-pounders, 3 3-pounders, and 2 machine guns. We are told that she is old and obsolete. My hon. friend the Minister of Naval Service (Mr. Hazen) rolled like a sweet morsel on his tongue the statement mad,e by Commander Roper that these vessels, the plans of which had been prepared by the British Admiralty in 1911, and for which the contracts could have been let in October, 1911, by the minister himself, would be obsolete before they could be constructed. If that statement is true, then nearly the whole British navy is obsolete. It is a statement which could be made in regard to every vessel that is over two or three years old, to ,every vessel, that is to say, that was constructed prior to 1910 or 1911. That is the proposition of the hon. minister.
The ships which the British Admiralty built to take the places of our three dreadnoughts are not obsolete.
They have been built within the last three years, and they were not built to take the place of my hon. friend's dreadnoughts at all.
Yes, they were.
The British Admiralty simply proceeded in the ordinary course to construct those vessels.

Will my hon. friend permit me to put him right? A question was asked by Mr. Arthur Lee in the British House of Commons on 5th June, 1913, and in reply Mr. Churchill said:
The situation created by the rejection of the Canadian Naval Aid Bill requires immediate action in order that the margins of naval strength necessary for the whole world protection of the British Empire may he adequately ' maintained for the autumn and winter of 1915, and in the spring of 1916. In these circumstances, the Government have determined to advance the construction of the three contract ships of this year's programme, and orders have been issued by the Admiralty which will ensure their being begun at the earliest possible date instead of in March next.

My hon. friend knows what that meant. It simply meant that the Admiralty intended to build three ships after my right hon. friend the Prime Minister went over there and said: We will give you three ships, or rather we will borrow the money for you; and, when the British Admiralty found that he was not going to borrow the money, they had to build three ships in order to carry out their original programme.
They built them, and they are not obsolete.

What I was pointing cut was that the theory of my hon. friend the

"Minister of Marine and Fisheries that, because Commander Roper told him that the vessels, the plans of which had been drafted by the Admiralty in the winter of 1910-11, would be obsolete before they could be constructed, would apply to every vessel which vras constructed previous to three or four years ago.
If he told the truth.

How many naval vessels of the same class as the Niobe, and built in the same year, are now in commission in the British Navy? Seven, all built in the same year, and of the same class exactly. How many armoured ships older than the Niobe are there in the British Navy? There are no less than ten built at dates running back to 1895. They are as follows:
